articles.title: Russian Mi-28 Attack Helicopters Are Now Firing Cruise Missiles
articles.text:
Russia’s Defense Ministry has released footage showing a Mi-28NM Havoc attack helicopter firing a small, low-cost cruise missile, supposedly during combat operations in Ukraine. The video provides the clearest official indication yet that Russia is exploring a non-traditional new launch platform for its emerging family of relatively inexpensive standoff weapons.

One missile is seen being fired from a pylon beneath the helicopter’s left-side stub wing; the helicopter returns after the mission with an unfired missile still hanging under the right-side stub wing. The Defense Ministry has not provided a date, precise location, or details about the target. Nor has it identified the weapon, which could be either the S8000 Banderol or the Dan-T, two closely related and visually very similar Russian missile developments.

The footage is not entirely unexpected. Earlier this year, photographs began circulating showing a Mi-28NM on the ground, carrying what appeared to be the same missile. There had also been unconfirmed reports from Ukraine in August that Russia was using the helicopter as a launch platform for Banderol, including firing the weapons from over the Sea of Azov against targets around Odesa.

The Banderol, developed by Russia’s Kronstadt company, was first detailed by Ukrainian military intelligence (GUR) in the spring of 2025. According to GUR, the missile is approximately 16.4 feet long, has pop-out wings, and is powered by a small turbojet engine. It reportedly flies at around 310 miles per hour, has a range of up to 310 miles, and carries a warhead weighing approximately 110 pounds.

GUR’s analysis also provided a detailed rundown of the foreign components it identified in the weapon. Its production involves “around 30 companies” supplying “more than 20 key components,” with potentially additional parts that have yet to be identified. Among the components reportedly used are a small commercial Chinese SW800Pro turbojet and a Russian-made Kometa digital antenna for satellite navigation. The weapon also makes extensive use of components sourced from foreign manufacturers, including in the United States.

The other possible candidate is the Dan-T, apparently derived from the Dan-M target drone, but with a roughly 300-pound warhead added. It is also reported to have a range of around 310 miles, while costing approximately 35 percent less than the Banderol.

The Banderol first emerged publicly through Ukrainian intelligence reporting, but Moscow eventually began acknowledging the weapon. Russian state television showed it beneath the wing of a Kronstadt Orion drone in July 2026, when it was first officially presented, albeit heavily obscured.

Ukrainian reporting indicates that the weapon has already seen operational use. Between mid-May and mid-July, the Ukrainian Air Force recorded 16 strikes involving Banderol. It reported five launches in a single barrage on July 16.

There are also indications that the Dan-T could ultimately become the more widely procured weapon. Reports from Ukraine suggest that Russia’s Aerospace Forces may have decided to focus procurement on the Dan-T, with plans to acquire tens of thousands of the missiles. Unlike the Banderol, the Dan-T is also reportedly intended for launch from combat aircraft and ground-based launchers. In September, Russia was already pitching the weapon for export at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt.

The use of a helicopter to launch a weapon of this type is particularly unusual. A relatively slow- and low-flying platform like the Mi-28 would be much more vulnerable to enemy air defenses than a fixed-wing tactical aircraft. However, the reported range of the Banderol and Dan-T would allow the helicopter to launch well away from the intended target, potentially from across the border while remaining in Russian airspace. For comparison, the maximum range of the Kh-38 (or LMUR) missile — which is otherwise the farthest-reaching Mi-28 weapon — is a little over nine miles.

For many months now, Russia has been seeking to expand its arsenal of weapons capable of striking Ukrainian targets from standoff distances. Mounting losses of Russian tactical aircraft to Ukrainian ground-based air defenses have underscored the need for weapons that can hit targets precisely at and well behind the front lines without exposing expensive aircraft to excessive risk.

Most notably, Russia has fielded the UMPK, a fairly crude type of guided glide bomb that has caused considerable difficulties for Ukrainian air defenses since its introduction around early 2023. The UMPK series has since been followed by more refined winged precision-guided glide bombs.

However, these weapons are unpowered. The small turbojet engine fitted to the Banderol and Dan-T puts them in the cruise missile category, while their reported range of up to 310 miles is particularly significant, if accurate. That range comes at the expense of warhead size, especially when compared with larger Russian cruise missiles.

The weapons’ navigation and electronic warfare protection systems are also important considerations. An inertial navigation system, combined with a jamming-resistant satellite navigation system, should provide a degree of resilience against the kind of electronic warfare jamming that is increasingly being employed by Ukraine. Satellite navigation can also help correct for accumulated drift, an important consideration given the accuracy limitations of inertial navigation systems over longer distances.

In essence, the Banderol and Dan-T offer Russia a lower-cost, potentially higher-volume complement to its more sophisticated cruise missiles.

As we noted previously:

“The Banderol is particularly relevant in the context of the economics of the Ukraine conflict. Russian forces have increasingly used combinations of relatively inexpensive one-way attack drones and more expensive cruise and ballistic missiles. The drones can be produced in large numbers and used to complicate air-defense operations, while the more capable missiles provide greater speed, range, payload, or penetration capability. A small turbojet-powered weapon such as Banderol offers another point on that spectrum.”

The ability to launch these weapons from non-traditional platforms, including drones, attack helicopters, and potentially ground-based systems, would also give Russia greater flexibility in how it employs them. Its bomber fleets and fixed-wing tactical aircraft could concentrate on their primary roles and make use of their established weapons, while other platforms take on some of the standoff strike mission.

For the Mi-28NM, meanwhile, the ability to employ a long-range cruise missile could provide a useful additional role, particularly after the helicopter fleet has suffered heavy losses during the war in Ukraine.

According to the Oryx open-source tracking group, Russia has lost 21 Mi-28s since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine four years ago. This figure could be higher because Oryx only tabulates losses it can confirm visually. Russia began the conflict with a force of around 110 Mi-28s of all versions. Other Russian battlefield helicopter types have suffered even heavier attrition, reflecting the level of danger that rotorcraft are exposed to when close to the front lines.

Russia is not alone in exploring this concept. The U.S. Marine Corps is working to give its AH-1Z Viper attack helicopters a new long-range strike capability through L3Harris’ modular Red Wolf launched-effects family. The weapon, which has already been test-fired from an AH-1Z, is being developed under the Marines’ Long Range Attack Missile (LRAM) effort, with a reported range in the low hundreds of miles. Beyond its kinetic strike role, Red Wolf can also be configured for missions such as communications relay and electronic warfare and has also been pitched for U.S. Army helicopters and tiltrotors. The effort reflects a broader push to give rotary-wing aircraft the ability to deliver precision effects well beyond the range of their traditional weapons, while raising questions about where the boundaries between cruise missiles, drones, and other launched effects are increasingly drawn.

For the Kremlin, the appeal of such weapons lies not only in their relatively low cost, but also in the ability to field them across a wider variety of platforms, further complicating Ukraine’s efforts to deal with incoming attacks.

articles.title: Wisconsin reports measles death of a baby, first death in over 35 years
articles.text:
An infant in Wisconsin has died of measles, the first measles death in the state since 1990, officials reported Thursday. The death comes amid an outbreak in the badger state that has stricken over 430 people across 13 counties this year.

"Any death of a child is a tragedy, and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Wisconsin Health Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family."

The baby's death is the third measles fatality nationally just this week, following the death of a New York child reported on Monday and another death in Pennsylvania reported on Wednesday. The Pennsylvania death was of an unvaccinated person in Jefferson County; the state health department did not provide additional details, such as the age of the person. The state's explosive, ongoing measles outbreak has led to 1,467 cases so far this year.

articles.title: Mac lookalikes multiply as Linux raids Apple's wardrobe
articles.text:
Linux can do many things, but good looks aren't always its strong point. Apple has rather more of a reputation in that department, and a crop of new projects is bringing Mac-style polish to the open source desktop.

Some are all-new, such as the Argentinian Lord OS, a whole new GUI desktop on top of Debian. Another, Cutefish, is a revival of a pre-ChatGPT project that never got as far as a complete release. Now it has version 1.0 for both x86-64 and Arm64, plus it's working on Mac binary compatibility via a work-in-progress layer called Reef. Ukrainian Desert OS is already at version 5.5 – practically a venerable elder in this company, despite appearing to be only about a year old.

Meanwhile, ClokeOS uses Xfce for its desktop, but underneath, the OS is based on Apple's FOSS XNU kernel. The project lead plans to offer compatibility with multiple types of binaries: Linux apps, plus Mac apps via Darling, and Windows apps via Wine.

This isn't new. Much as Cutefish has been revived, last year we reported on PearOS Linux, a very Mac-like skin on KDE Plasma. It has hooks in place for ambitious future features, such as Siri-style speech recognition.

What's striking is the number of projects appearing and the pace of their development. Some offer both x86-64 and Arm64 builds, with Raspberry Pi editions in certain cases. For human coders, this would be months of hard work, but if it's just checking an additional box in an LLM development tool, then why wouldn't you? It's almost no extra work, but it widens the potential audience.

Coveting Mac-like good looks is a longstanding urge among Linux users, and with legitimate reason. There's nothing wrong with Macs, even if you are mainly a FOSS user. Modern macOS, or OS X as it was called a decade ago, is a Unix underneath its shiny proprietary desktop, and many of the flagship Linux FOSS apps also have Mac versions, from Firefox and Thunderbird, via LibreOffice, to VirtualBox, plus less well-known but very handy apps such as Ferdium and Panwriter. We've written about the usefulness of FOSS apps on macOS before, including for reviving elderly Macs.

Just a couple of months ago, we published a two-part guide on how to give Xfce a macOS-like layout and then how to tweak it so apps fit in better. We focused on the functionality, though, not the looks – we don't really care much for such things. If it does matter to you, though, you're not alone, and there are lots of themes and skins to make Xfce look prettier.

Some of these are all-in-one packages that you can install on an existing distro to give it a new look. One recent example is Cupertino, developed with assistance from Claude. From a few years ago, there are Small Sur and Ventura-Xfce. From nine years ago, long pre-LLM, there is osXFCE.

We can see the appeal. From 2006 to 2020, Macs used Intel x86 processors, and those machines are now all falling off the end of Apple support – only four Intel models supported last year's macOS 26 "Tahoe," support for which is just starting to reach OpenCore Legacy Patcher. Earlier this year, The Reg FOSS desk upgraded his 11-year-old iMac to macOS 15 "Sequoia" with OCLP 2.5.1. The first experimental OCLP 3.0 release appeared last month, and it's now up to 3.0-rc5. This adds support for macOS 26, Apple's final major macOS release for Intel Macs. That puts a ceiling on future macOS upgrades for both home-built Hackintoshes and older Macs kept going with unofficial patches.

We gave LordOS a brief spin using its OVA virtual machine image. It installed and booted without trouble, and looks impressive. Last month, we wrote about ZacOS-9 and Mavernix, and similarly, we gave ZacOS-9 a very quick spin in a VM. The resemblance to our recent experience with ZacOS-9 went beyond appearances. In both, we found that the keyboard UI is largely missing: standard keystrokes didn't work. In LordOS, we found some menu options duplicated in two places in an un-Mac-like way, such as "About" options in both the app menu and the Help menu. The LordOS GitHub repository does not credit any LLM assistants, but it's gone though nine test releases in three weeks.

The inevitable end of life of x86 Macs is driving fresh interest in FOSS OSes. They offer a life extension for genuine Macs as well as the enticing prospect of Mac-like polish for existing FOSS OSes. Combine that with the fast, easy code generation offered by LLM coding assistants, and we think there's going to be a lot more of this. In 2025, we saw one macOS-like Linux project rebooted. This October, we saw two new ones. In November, we've found four more. We have a feeling that these are just the first trickles of what may soon become a flood. ®

articles.title: Oak Ridge labs gets hybrid quantum-HPC system to test qubit error correction
articles.text:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) now boasts a system for research into quantum error correction, combining IBM quantum processors with a high-performance compute (HPC) system based on AMD silicon.

The Quantum Science Center (QSC) at ORNL, funded by the US Department of Energy (DoE), unveiled what it calls a co-design platform for quantum error correction, marrying up quantum and HPC technology.

While useful, fault-tolerant quantum systems always seem to be at least a decade away, there have been notable advances over the past several years in the field of quantum error correction, according to ORNL. These include early demonstrations of protecting quantum information from environmental noise, which can cause loss of the fragile quantum states needed for computations.

"Solving the challenges of quantum error correction is essential to making quantum computing a practical tool for scientific discovery, which is a priority for Oak Ridge National Laboratory," said QSC director Travis Humble.

IBM Fellow and director of IBM Research Jay Gambetta said that it was no longer a question of whether error correction works, but how to accelerate and optimize error correction to build systems that scientists can use to tackle challenging problems.

"This new co-design platform for quantum error correction allows us to evaluate different approaches and determine the architectures, software and workflows that will scale," he stated.

ORNL's new tool combines an IBM Quantum System Two, equipped with the latest 120-qubit Nighthawk r2 quantum processors, and Umbra, a classical HPC system powered by AMD 5th Gen Epyc CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators.

According to AMD, the CPUs provide the orchestration and general-purpose performance needed to coordinate everything, while the GPUs accelerate simulation, optimization and the parallel scientific computations surrounding quantum workloads.

Also part of the system are AMD Versal SoCs to provide the low-latency control, readout and decoding capabilities for the quantum circuitry.

ORNL says that this brings together the computing infrastructure needed for quantum error correction in a single environment, and opens it up to more researchers than ever before. They will use it to develop and validate quantum algorithms, workflows, and applications in an environment built for quantum-centric supercomputing, an emerging paradigm where quantum processors (QPUs), CPUs, and GPUs work together as one system.

IBM says that one promising approach the co-design platform cloud explore is hierarchical error correction. It describes this as using an inner code to protect qubits within a module, while an outer code wraps around the inner code’s logical qubits and adds a second layer of protection.

This approach could reach a trillion logical operations at a physical error rate of one in a thousand, IBM research suggested. These hierarchical codes rely on having powerful classical compute, and the co-design platform will give researchers a place to test and develop those ideas with GPUs in a low-latency environment, the firm states.

The co-design platform is likely to play a key part in the DoE’s Quantum Genesis Mission objectives. These include the recently announced Q Competition, an initiative to deliver a system with 100 logical qubits capable of performing hundreds of millions of fault-tolerant operations. It follows an executive order from President Trump to develop a full-blown quantum system by 2028.®

articles.title: Agnipath scheme threatened national security, was introduced in haste: Congress’s Rohit Chaudhary
articles.text:
Agnipath scheme threatened national security, was introduced in haste: Congress’s Rohit Chaudhary
Congress demanded the scrapping of the Agnipath scheme, alleging that it weakens national security and disrupts military training and cadre management.
Congress on Friday demanded the scrapping of the Agnipath recruitment scheme, alleging that it weakens national security, disrupts military training and leaves young recruits without the job security and benefits available to regular soldiers.
“This was a major scheme that threatened to weaken our national security. The Modi government introduced it in haste, without adequate consideration,” Congress leader Colonel (Retd.) Rohit Chaudhary said.
Introduced in June 2022, the Agnipath scheme recruits personnel below officer rank for four years, with 25% of each batch eligible for retention in regular service. On November 4, the Union Cabinet approved an additional two-year engagement period for the remaining 75% of the recruited pool, after which they can be considered for regular enrolment subject to their willingness and meeting selection criteria. The move came weeks before more than 18,300 Agniveers from the first batch were due to complete their four-year tenure by December 31.
Deep Dive
Chaudhary questioned why the government was extending the service period instead of regularising all Agniveers. Referring to the Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani’s assessment that recruits had performed well, he asked, “If all of them performed so well, why are only 25% being made regular soldiers today? Why should the remaining 75 % have to wait?”
Arguing that the scheme could undermine operational preparedness, Chaudhary said, “We do not need a contractual army to guard these borders. We need a regular army.” He alleged that the short tenure had disrupted cadre management and limited opportunities for further training, especially for technical roles in the armed forces. “Over four years, we are unable to provide these recruits with the proper training required under the army’s established system,” he said.
“When you do not even know whether a person will remain in service after four years, the entire training system is disrupted,” said Colonel Sudhir from the Congress’s ex-servicemen department.
Lieutenant Colonel Navjot Singh Thind, who heads the party’s ex-servicemen department in Chandigarh, said there had been no need to alter the army’s recruitment system. “As a soldier, I certainly know that there was absolutely no need to tamper with the army in this manner. And if there was a need to do so, why have they now changed the scheme?” he asked.
Chaudhary also alleged that Agniveers faced unequal treatment compared with regular soldiers in terms of pay, leave, career progression and compensation for those killed in service. “Agniveers are given only 30 days of leave, whereas regular soldiers are entitled to 90 days…Living and working in such a stressful environment became extremely difficult for them,” he added.
He further called for families of Agniveers killed in the line of duty to receive lifelong pensions and benefits equivalent to those provided to families of regular soldiers.
The Congress leader said the revised service tenure for Agniveers was an acknowledgement by the BJP-led government of the scheme’s failure. “It [BJP] has effectively admitted that the Agnipath scheme was an unlawful, ill-conceived, unwarranted, anti-national, anti-military and anti-youth decision that needed to be rejected,” he said.
Chaudhary further announced the launch of “Jai Jawan Part Two”, renewing the Congress’s campaign against the Agnipath scheme. Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi launched the “Jai Jawan” campaign in 2024, demanding the scrapping of the Agnipath scheme and the restoration of regular army recruitment.

articles.title: Manipur’s CoTU pauses shutdown over 2 Kuki youths’ killing, gives government 7 days to act
articles.text:
Manipur’s CoTU pauses shutdown over 2 Kuki youths’ killing, gives government 7 days to act
Manipur’s Kuki-Zo body CoTU has suspended the Kangpokpi shutdown for seven days, giving the state government time to meet demands over the killing of two Kuki youths.
A Kuki-Zo body in Manipur’s Kangpokpi district, the Committee on Tribal Unity (CoTU), on Friday announced a seven-day suspension of the ongoing shutdown to give the state government time to address its demands over the abduction and killing of two Kuki youths. The committee, however, warned that it would resume the shutdown and intensify its agitation if the government failed to meet its demands within the deadline.
The committee issued a statement on Friday saying that the decision came amid tensions in Kangpokpi district following the alleged abduction of two Kuki youths from Taphou Kuki village on October 28 and the subsequent discovery of their mutilated bodies on November 1.
Since the recovery of the bodies, CoTU had been imposing a total shutdown, which had been extended repeatedly.
The statement further said that sit-ins would be organised at various locations during the seven-day period. The committee also decided not to accept the bodies, which are still lying at the morgue, until its charter of demands is fulfilled.
The committee warned that if the government failed to fulfil its demands within the seven days, CoTU would resume the shutdown along with other intensified forms of agitation.
The two Kuki youths, Paoginlal Hangshing (20) and Tinginlun Chongloi (21), went missing at around 5.30pm on October 28 after reportedly being abducted by unidentified people while travelling.
National Highway-2 (Imphal-Dimapur) passes through the Kangpokpi district headquarters. The highway has been disrupted by protesters since 5pm on October 29.
Their mutilated bodies were found during an extensive joint search operation on November 1 by joint teams comprising Manipur Police, the Commando Battalion for Resolute Action (CoBRA), the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), the Assam Rifles and the Rapid Action Force (RAF) in the general area east of NH-2, along the Senapati-Phaibung Road.
Manipur Police Headquarters also issued a statement on Friday, saying that the cases related to the recent incidents of arson and killings of civilians were under thorough investigation. Efforts were being made to identify the accused, while witnesses were being located and questioned.
The statement further said that joint teams of the police, CoBRA, CRPF, the BSF (Border Security Force), the Assam Rifles and the Army were conducting cordon and search operations (CASOs) as well as intelligence-based operations in the affected areas to take action in accordance with the law and punish those responsible for the crimes.
“Necessary action is also being taken up with the National Investigation Agency (NIA)…Police and all security forces are taking the matter with utmost concern. Security measures have been put in place, and the situation is being closely monitored,” the statement said.
Officials said the post-mortems of the two deceased had been conducted at the Regional Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS), Imphal, and that the bodies were still lying at the hospital morgue.
The Manipur Police has appealed to the public to remain calm, exercise restraint and not take the law into their own hands. People have been asked not to believe or circulate unverified information, rumours or provocative content on social media that may escalate tension and violence.

articles.title: Pakistan says willing to issue visa to Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann for visit
articles.text:
Pakistan says willing to issue visa to Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann for visit
Pakistan Foreign Office said it would consider a visa for Bhagwant Mann if he wishes to visit, adding whether India allows him to travel is a separate matter.
Pakistan on Friday said it would consider issuing a visa to Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann if the Indian politician wished to visit the country.
Pakistan Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan made the remarks during his weekly media briefing in response to a question about the possible visit of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) leader.
The Pakistani government would "consider issuing him a visa if he wished to visit the country", Khan said, clarifying that whether the Indian government permits Mann to travel to Pakistan was an entirely separate matter.
On October 23, Mann had said that he had been invited to attend the World Punjabi Conference in Lahore on November 27.
However, he questioned whether he would be allowed to travel to Pakistan.
"Our culture is the same. Many poets from here will go there," he had said.
Mann had also expressed his desire that all legislators of the Punjab legislative assembly visit Kartarpur Sahib in Pakistan if the Kartarpur Corridor reopened.
The corridor, which connects Dera Baba Nanak in India's Punjab with the historic Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur, Pakistan, was established to facilitate Sikh pilgrims travelling to the shrine associated with Guru Nanak Dev, the founder of Sikhism.
It allows Indian pilgrims to visit the gurdwara without requiring a visa for Pakistan, subject to the applicable arrangements.
The corridor has remained closed to pilgrim movement from the Indian side since May 7, 2025, when India launched pre-dawn missile strikes on nine terror targets in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir following the Pahalgam terror attack.
Pakistan said it remained ready to facilitate pilgrims once the restrictions were lifted.

articles.title: Strike drones launched from British aircraft carrier for the first time
articles.text:
The Royal Navy has successfully launched strike drones from an aircraft carrier for the first time, in a major step towards transforming how Britain fights at sea.

Royal Navy press release

In landmark North Atlantic trials, which took place in mid-October, British made Nyan Maritime one-way drones, manufactured in Wiltshire by Callen-Lenz, took off from HMS Queen Elizabeth’s flight deck, demonstrating how autonomous strike systems could operate alongside F-35B stealth jets.

The trials mark another step towards the Navy’s high-tech approach to fighting in the air, from an aircraft carrier, known as the ‘hybrid carrier air wing’. It brings together crewed aircraft and drones to increase the carrier’s reach, lethality and flexibility, while keeping personnel further away from danger.

The trials developed understanding how uncrewed strike systems could contribute to future Carrier Strike operations and wider Defence activity.

Working with experts from across the Armed Forces and industry, the Royal Navy conducted a number of flights from HMS Queen Elizabeth, following the drone’s first launch at sea from experimentation ship XV Patrick Blackett earlier this year.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said:

“The threat environment we are facing is fundamentally different from that of recent decades. A major determinant of military power now is who can innovate fastest.

“This first for the Royal Navy shows how we’re using the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War to invest in equipment and technology that gives our forces greater reach to strike the enemy, with increased lethality.

“The more ready we are to fight and win, the less likely we are to have to. This investment strengthens our warfighting readiness and therefore our deterrence.”

At the same time, the carrier hosted Heavy Lift Challenge 3, which saw a Tekever AR5 fixed-wing uncrewed aircraft operate from a carrier for the first time.

With a 7m wingspan and capacity to carry 80kg, the AR5 can support both logistics and operational missions. The trials demonstrated how drones used for intelligence, surveillance, target acquisition and reconnaissance could operate alongside strike systems as part of a more integrated fighting force.

Together, the trials demonstrate how uncrewed aircraft can increase the flexibility and capability of the UK’s aircraft carriers as the Royal Navy develops its future hybrid air wing.

Lieutenant Commander David Burton, trials sponsor for Navy Capability, said:

“These trials give us the evidence and confidence to decide how uncrewed systems can work alongside crewed aircraft.

“The lessons will help us build a hybrid Navy that gives commanders greater choice and ensures our carriers remain at the cutting edge of naval warfare.”

The trials are part of the government’s plan to modernise the Armed Forces for the way wars are fought today. The Defence Investment Plan provides over £5bn for autonomous systems by 2030, the largest ever drone investment in Defence.

The plan includes:

  • almost £250m for Project Pantheon, developing autonomous systems to build a hybrid carrier air wing, and for trials of jet-powered drones to work alongside the F-35B force
  • at least £1.3bn for a hybrid fleet of crewed and uncrewed ships, with the first large autonomous vessels due in service by 2030
  • at least £210m for low-cost, long-range one-way attack drones for the Navy, Army, and RAF

The plan also sets out that the Queen Elizabeth class carriers will use uncrewed systems to strengthen the F-35B force, creating a hybrid carrier air wing.

“These trials give us the evidence and confidence to decide how uncrewed systems can work alongside crewed aircraft.”

articles.title: RIP to the world’s ugliest car
articles.text:
Elon Musk has hit the brakes on the Cybertruck, announcing on X that Tesla will wind down production at its Texas factory around mid-2027.

Despite years of delays, the stainless-steel turd Musk claimed was a futuristic, apocalypse-proof tank straight out of Blade Runner is headed for a production wind-down after roughly four years, putting the Cybertruck alongside such automotive flops as the Edsel and the DeLorean.

We can’t even put the Cybertruck on the same tier as the Ford Pinto, as that deathtrap was produced for a decade.

The first Cybertruck lumbered off Tesla’s production line in mid-2023 before going on sale later that year, and it was practically right out of the gate that the problems began.

Within months of the first deliveries, recall notices began piling up on the monstrosity. Trim pieces were flying off, internal components were failing, cameras were malfunctioning – all in all, the thing has faced 11 recalls since hitting the road in late 2023, most recently in April 2026, when a defect in brake rotors was found to potentially cause cracks that could allow wheel studs to separate from their hubs.

Musk had pinned a lot of Tesla's hopes on the Cybertruck a few years ago, describing it during the company's Q3 2023 earnings call as "a great product" that would eventually generate "significant positive cash flow" for Tesla.

Musk said on that same earnings call that Tesla intended to ramp Cybertruck production up to 250,000 vehicles per year by 2025 to meet the over one million Cybertruck reservations he claimed Tesla had taken. Some Musk fans may still be waiting for their Cybertrucks, while others may have canceled their reservations after reading early reviews or experiencing the reality of driving such an ugly vehicle associated with a right-wing provocateur. Tesla hasn't disclosed how many reservations were canceled or converted into sales.

Even then, it was widely reported in recent years that unsold Cybertrucks were piling up around the US, with Tesla unable to move them even with repeated price reductions. Tesla has never shared Cybertruck sales numbers, but it’s estimated that only around 70,000 of the things have been sold in the past three years - not exactly a ringing endorsement of its marketability.

So that’s that for the Cybertruck - it’s safe to say it’s been a total disaster for Musk and Tesla. It never sold well, never became a boat, and will likely never be remembered fondly. ®

articles.text:
Supreme Court appoints ex-CJI Gavai to head panel scrutinising forest rights claims in Tamil Nadu
The Supreme Court has tasked a panel led by ex-CJI Bhushan Gavai with scrutinising forest rights claims under the FRA in Tamil Nadu.
The Supreme Court on Friday appointed former Chief Justice of India (CJI) Bhushan R Gavai to head a special committee that will scrutinise orders passed by authorities in Tamil Nadu under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 (FRA), even as it came down hard on the state government for its prolonged failure to initiate the statutory process to identify and adjudicate the claims of forest dwellers in the ecologically sensitive Agasthyamalai landscape.
A bench of justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta constituted the committee, comprising Justice Gavai as chairperson, an officer of the Central Empowered Committee (CEC) and Tamil Nadu’s principal chief conservator of forests, to oversee the determination of claims by Forest-Dwelling Scheduled Tribe (FDST) and other traditional forest dwellers (OTFD). The committee will scrutinise the orders passed by competent authorities under the FRA and submit its findings to the court in a sealed cover.
The court directed the state to complete the constitution of the remaining Gram Sabhas within 30 days and conclude the entire process of inviting and adjudicating claims through the statutory three-tier mechanism within five months of their constitution. The committee, in turn, has been asked to complete its scrutiny within two months of the expiry of this outer deadline.
Criticising the state for its inaction, the bench observed that the process under the FRA had remained uninitiated for years even after an interim stay imposed by the Madras high court was vacated by the Supreme Court in 2016.
“Apparently thus, the process under Section 6 was never initiated for years even after the lifting of the stay and seems to have been triggered only after this Court took suo motu cognizance of the prevailing situation,” it said.
The bench added that the state appeared to have “woken up” only after the court directed the removal of encroachments from the Srivilliputhur-Megamalai Tiger Reserve and other reserved forests in the Agasthyamalai Biosphere.
“It is clear that the State Government is primarily responsible for the delay in the process of receiving, identifying and adjudicating the claims under the FRA, 2006. Before this Court took cognizance of the encroachments in the forest area, even the Gram Sabhas had not been constituted,” said the bench, granting the state what it described as a “last opportunity” to complete the exercise.
The committee has been empowered to issue necessary directions to authorities for expeditious disposal of claims. The state will also have to submit monthly progress reports to it.
Senior counsel Jaideep Gupta appeared for the state government, while senior advocate Sriram Panchu represented the state’s department of Social Justice.
The directions came in proceedings concerning large-scale encroachments in the Agasthyamalai landscape, where the court had, in its May 29 judgment, ordered a structured and time-bound process for eviction, rehabilitation and ecological restoration. The latest proceedings arose from competing claims over the application of the FRA to people residing in or cultivating land in the Megamalai region.
While the state argued that claims under the FRA needed to be examined before eviction, the court accepted the amicus curiae and senior advocate K Parmeshwar’s submission that the statutory protection could not be extended indiscriminately to everyone occupying or cultivating forest land.
The bench clarified that two categories of occupants identified by the state itself would be excluded from consideration under the Act. These are people cultivating forest land while maintaining only temporary residence within it and those residing outside the forest boundary but cultivating land inside it.
The state’s affidavit had identified 4,594 occupants spread across 5,072.64 hectares, of whom 2,643 were engaged in silk cotton cultivation over 3,637.83 hectares. Of these, 1,595 persons were permanently residing in the forest and cultivating land, 232 had temporary residence while cultivating, and 2,767 were residing outside the forest boundary but cultivating within it.
The court said the latter two categories could not qualify as FDST or OTFD merely on the basis of cultivation, since the statutory definitions required claimants to primarily reside in and depend on forest land. For OTFDs, the law specifically requires residence and dependence for at least three generations, or 75 years, prior to December 13, 2005.
The court also rejected the state’s attempt to justify silk cotton cultivation as a traditional minor forest produce protected under the FRA. It noted that the government had relied on historical cultivation and agricultural records but had failed to produce any specific notification recognising silk cotton as minor forest produce under the Act or any other forest law.
Distinguishing between naturally occurring forest produce and commercial cultivation, the bench said the material suggested that silk cotton had been introduced as a planned plantation rather than traditionally collected as minor forest produce.
“The concept of planned cultivation of commercial crop is totally contrary to the very concept of a naturally occurring minor forest produce,” said the bench, adding that commercial crop cultivation could not become a recognised forest right to justify continued occupation of reserved forest land.
It further asked the CEC to examine the state’s claim that silk cotton qualified as minor forest produce and investigate the circumstances surrounding cultivation by people residing outside the forest boundary, including whether others were financing or facilitating such activity.
The matter will next be heard on February 1, 2027, when the court will consider an interim status report.

articles.title: DoJ's 'Super Intelligence Task Force' up and running
articles.text:
The US Department of Justice (DoJ) says its Super Intelligence Task Force (SINTF) is now up and running, after president Donald Trump ordered the move in a memo last month.

Headed up by director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, as well as associate attorney general Stanley Woodward and associate deputy attorney general Stephen Weiss, SINTF's responsibility is to protect the US's lead in artificial intelligence development.

Thursday's announcement, which was littered with the "super intelligence" Trumpism, said the task force will ensure the US's SI/AI leadership remains uncompromised by foreign AI "abuse," including by state and state-backed groups, criminal enterprises, individuals, or corporate entities.

Per Trump's October 13 memo [PDF], SITF will take "affirmative measures, as appropriate," to ensure the US stays ahead in AI development. It did not elaborate on what this nebulous phrase meant, but it can be reasonably assumed this means a breadth of proactive steps.

The memo also stated that the task force will organize the DoJ's criminal and civil lawsuits involving AI, recommend enforcement priorities concerning public safety and AI misuse, develop prosecution guidance for unlawful AI conduct, and feed into legislative proposals to prevent "burdensome regulation."

Addressing a Wall Street Journal tech conference this week, Pentagon CTO and SITF vice chair Emil Michael said the team would release details about its AI regulatory landscape later this month.

The task force will also shoulder various cross-departmental responsibilities, such as "deconflicting investigations, cases, and other matters" among departments and the offices of US attorneys.

According to quotes from senior officials, chief among the concerns facing ordinary US citizens are AI attacks that target individuals, as well as those that aim to disrupt critical infrastructure and other national security interests.

"The creation of the DOJ-SITF marks an important moment for the Department to help advance SI technologies and, at the same time, protect American innovation," said Weiss.

"The Department also has a responsibility to utilize law enforcement tools at our disposal to deter improper use of SI, harden regular reporting on SI risk and response, and ensure companies exercise vigorous internal controls so that SI technology behaves as intended. The Department is committed to protecting all Americans and our business interests."

Trump compelled the US to start using the term "super intelligence" in September, claiming "artificial intelligence," the widely used and original term coined in the mid-1950s, was a better descriptor for the technology's capabilities.

The US government's dedicated website for SI states that "America is in a race for Super Intelligence. We intend to win it."

It also highlights a number of initiatives the government has taken to promote its AI supremacy, including legal guidance to streamline federal approvals, leading to more data centers being built.

The pivot toward renaming the technology in all official capacities raised confusion at the time.

A somewhat contradictory move, the Trump administration heavily promotes its own AI innovators, but in one swoop essentially antiquated the trading name of arguably its most recognizable AI lab, OpenAI.

One financier previously floated the idea that Trump ordered the shift to boost the value of .si domain names, many of which have recently been registered using MAGA-related terms and resold for millions of dollars. There is no categorical evidence that the investments are linked to the Trump family, however. ®

Kerala’s Forest Department has ordered the airlift of an 18-month-old elephant calf, Maya, from Abhayaranyam to Vantara in Jamnagar for specialised medical care after she suffered multiple fractures and severe bone weakness.
Kerala Chief Wildlife Warden Dr P Pugazhendi, IFS, ordered her transfer on November 5, following consultations with veterinary experts who recommended exploring further treatment options before considering euthanasia.

Abandoned at birth, rescued by forest staff
Maya was rescued on April 19, 2025, after being found abandoned near Kaprikkad in the Malayattoor Division. Her herd had crossed a river without her, leaving the newborn calf weak and severely dehydrated. As she had no suckling reflex, forest staff had to hand-rear her under round-the-clock supervision.
Assistant Forest Veterinary Officer Dr Binoy C Babu and other caregivers looked after her, with a Medical Board monitoring her health and treating several complications.
Her condition deteriorated after she slipped while playing on July 2 this year, injuring her right shoulder. Despite treatment, physiotherapy and calcium and vitamin D supplementation, she developed multiple fractures and eventually lost the ability to stand.
An examination on October 24 by a veterinary expert from the College of Veterinary and Animal Sciences, Pookode, found a fractured left humerus, multiple fractures in the right radius, generalised bone thinning, a chest infection and pressure sores.
The Medical Board subsequently recommended euthanasia, citing her grave prognosis and extremely brittle bones.
However, during consultations on November 4, Padma Shri Dr Kushal Konwar Sarma, an elephant veterinarian from Assam and Veterinary Advisor to Vantara, identified a possible parathyroid-related disorder that could respond to treatment. Vantara's Head Veterinarian Dr Yaduraj Khadpekar supported transferring her for intensive care.
At Vantara, Maya will receive round-the-clock monitoring, pain management and advanced diagnostics. Three Vantara elephant veterinarians, along with paravets and caregivers, will accompany her during the airlift. Her familiar caregiver and Kerala forest veterinarian will also travel with her.
A Kerala Monitoring Committee will oversee her progress, and Vantara will facilitate her return to Abhayaranyam after treatment. Her prognosis remains uncertain.

EC gives fresh chance to voters excluded from draft SIR rolls in Delhi, Maharashtra, 5 other states
The EC has directed seven states to help electors marked absent, shifted, dead or duplicate submit fresh forms and seek inclusion in final rolls.
Most of the electors struck off draft rolls during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) can now seek re-inclusion without filing Form 6, the Election Commission of India (ECI) said on Friday. The Form 6 route remains available, it clarified, but it is not the only option.
In a letter dated November 6, addressed to the chief electoral officers (CEOs) of Delhi, Maharashtra, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Telangana and Nagaland, the Commission said electors marked Absent, Shifted, Dead or Duplicate (ASDD), and thus excluded from the draft roll, will get “one more opportunity” to be included in the final roll. Accepted applicants will get the same EPIC number they held before the SIR, indicating they are being treated as existing electors rather than first-time enrollees. These categories together account for around 130 million of the 134 million people struck off the rolls.
ALSO READ | High-rises to workplaces, UP casts wide net for unenrolled voters
“Booth-wise lists of all such electors, who were marked as absent, shifted, dead, or duplicate (ASDD) and whose enumeration forms were not received back and consequently could not be included in the Draft Electoral Roll during the ongoing SIR, shall be displayed afresh (once again) on the notice boards of the respective Polling Stations,” the letter stated.
A senior ECI official said this decision gives those left off the rolls one more chance to enroll. “Form6 will not be required in these cases at all. The process is much easier now. People can refill enumeration forms with the prescribed declaration,” this person added.
ALSO READ | Voters show enthusiasm as AMU students’ union polls return after 8 yrs
Form 6 is the statutory application under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, that eligible citizens use to be added to the electoral roll for the first time. Its declaration states that the applicant is enrolling for the first time and that their name is not already in any other constituency. False statements are punishable under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, with up to a year in jail, a fine, or both. The form became contentious during the SIR because electors left out of the draft who had been on the rolls for years had to seek inclusion afresh, although ECI clarified that doing this would not attract any punishment.
Friday’s order comes after weeks of scrutiny in the Supreme Court of Delhi’s roll, where the draft published on August 31 removed about 4.7 million names from roughly 14.5 million electors. On October 28, the bench hearing the case questioned why persons deleted from the draft roll should use Form 6 to register as new voters when they were on the rolls previously. Instead, it suggested that such voters be permitted to restore their names through Form 8, which is intended for address-related changes, or through the enumeration process. It also asked ECI to devise a mechanism to reach omitted voters, observing that the right to vote cannot be forfeited merely because a person was absent during enumeration.
But ECI still persevered with Form 6. On November 3, ECI clarified that deleted voters could file Form 6 to register as new voters. The poll panel said that voters whose names did not figure in the draft SIR rolls could submit Form 6 to seek fresh inclusion in the final voters’ list, even if they were enrolled previously. Citing a Delhi High Court’s October 14 judgment, the ECI said the apprehension of making a false declaration was misplaced.
A day before the ECI’s letter, the Bombay High Court also weighed in. A division bench of its Goa bench, comprising Justices Valmiki Menezes and Amit Jamsandekar, held on Thursday that existing voters who have only changed addresses cannot be compelled to file Form 6, which is meant for first-time registration, and must be allowed to file Form 8 even while the SIR is underway.
As per the ECI’s latest order, partially filled enumeration forms will be regenerated on the ECINET dashboard. District and electoral registration officers must try to reach electors through booth-level officers (BLOs) in person or via WhatsApp, email or SMS. BLOs are to make house-to-house visits in coordination with booth-level agents of political parties, and to ask neighbours, families and resident welfare associations. Electors can also download and fill the form online using their earlier EPIC number.
Electors who have not moved must submit the signed enumeration form with a statement explaining why they missed the earlier round, in person, through a family member, or online with e-sign. Those who shifted within the state need not file Form 8. They must submit the form, along with a statement and address proof to the electoral registration officer (ERO) of their new constituency. They can use the “Book a call with BLO” facility on the ECI website and app. For homeless people, a BLO’s field verification report will suffice as proof of residence.

The forms will be processed after verifying eligibility and residence, and accepted forms will be included in the final roll. Electors who have already filed Form 6 need not refile, and their applications will be processed under the Commission’s November 3 clarification.
Previously, the ECI extended the SIR schedule for these states on October 29 after requests from CEOs, following the Supreme Court’s request to consider extending the deadline for Delhi voters’ claims and objections. The schedule has been revised several times.

articles.title: Crowd fave Linux Mint update approaches, fresh from autumn release of Cinnamon desktop
articles.text:
Linux Mint 27 is expected next month, and it's starting to take shape. Its flagship desktop, Cinnamon 2.8, is already available.

The team behind the popular, beginner-friendly Linux just released Cinnamon 2.8, which will be the default desktop in Mint 27. Since 2014, Linux Mint versions have been based on the LTS releases of Ubuntu. Since a new LTS, Ubuntu 26.04 "Resolute Raccoon" arrived in late April, that means that a corresponding version of Mint is in development.

The Mint project blog post last month revealed the codename: "Adrien." This is the first male codename since Mint 1.0 "Ada" in 2006, based on the first ever Ubuntu LTS release, 6.06 "Dapper Drake", but the project has run through the whole alphabet since then (except for the letter “Y”.) That blog also revealed it will have a new alarm clock app, but the subsequent Mint Blog post imparted more information.

The Nemo file manager will gain a preview pane, there will be a new and much more capable system resource-monitor program called "Superlight", a new simple manager for compressed archive files (Zip and so on) called "Unfold," and a new, theme-able terminal emulator called "Velocitty." Mint also has a new Community Website, which uses GitHub to manage logins and eliminates the old website's dependency on PHP.

Probably the most significant new feature, though, is that Mint 27 will restore system hibernation. Ubuntu supported hibernation in its early releases, but it has been disabled as standard since 12.04 "Precise Pangolin." Enabling it again is regularly discussed, for instance back in 2020. As we discussed in some detail a year ago, it's a complicated subject and there's a lot that can go wrong.

It seems that Mint's Clément Lefebvre feels he can sort this, and we hope it works out. Support is included in the new version of Cinnamon, among a host of other changes. Its Wayland support is no longer experimental, although the X11 session is still there so users won't be forced to use the new system. The Network Manager applet has better, simpler VPN support and Wi-Fi encryption handling. There are multiple improvements across the desktop: better handling of sound devices, keyboard input layouts, touchpads and gesture support, HiDPI display handling, and better search in the Settings app. The window list control has been upgraded, more things happen in the background for faster desktop starts, and it has better handling and storage of authentication and credentials, including the same Rust-based "oo7" secret store we mentioned in Fedora 45. Screensaver handling is also mentioned – this is particularly problematic under Wayland, as XScreensaver maintainer Jamie Zawinski has covered with some feeling. The Mint blog mentioned this at the start of 2026, when Lefebvre announced the new, slower, annual release schedule.

LXQt 2.5

Cinnamon is not the only desktop environment that has moved to embrace Wayland while also maintaining its support for X.org. Almost exactly two years ago, we reported that the LXQt 2.1 included preliminary Wayland support. That project is very much still in active development, led by Jen-Lee "PCMan" Hong, and version 2.5.0 just appeared, almost simultaneously with Cinnamon 2.8.

Before LXQt, "PCMan" developed the LXDE desktop – which is still around. There's an LXDE spin of Fedora 45, the Raspberry Pi OS uses some of its components, and last year when Debian 13 was released we also noted that its terminal emulator, LXTerminal, had just been updated. This release of LXQt removes its last dependency on an LXDE component – until now, it still used the old menu-cache.

LXQt 2.5 is based on Qt 6.10, and it draws upon some of the components of KDE Plasma. One of these is libkscreen, which manages screens for Plasma. Version 6.8 of this drops X11 support – as does Plasma 6.8 itself – and that broke LXQt's Monitor Settings applet. The team are looking for a workaround and plan to fix this in a minor point release. Aside from this, the desktop's taskbar-style panel has improved sizing support, icon handling, and auto-hide, but most of the improvements in this release are in around its QTerminal terminal emulator.

New LXQt versions usually appear twice a year, around April and November, so this version will likely be in Lubuntu 27.04 in about five months – and available in many other distributions, too. ®

articles.text:
Jharkhand tribal leader dies by suicide after Facebook Live, blames Soren govt, land brokers
The nearly 11-minute video abruptly cuts off, with the camera appearing to be obstructed by a green object.
Tribal activist Nisha Kumari Bhagat allegedly died by suicide in Ranchi on Friday after going live on Facebook, accusing the state's Hemant Soren government and land brokers of harassing her.
In the purported live video, available on her Facebook profile, Bhagat is seen crying and alleging that anyone who raised their voice against "Hemant Soren government and its land brokers meant inviting death".
"I should have understood this earlier... People say there is BJP, there is Congress, but there is no one... My parents will be deeply hurt. My father played his role in the Jharkhand agitation. I tried very hard to fight the administration and also tried to talk to them about security... But today I have to embrace my own death because this Hemant Soren government can humiliate women, and I cannot bear this," she said in the video.
The nearly 11-minute video abruptly cuts off, with the camera appearing to be obstructed by a green object.
Police recover activist's body, investigation underway
SP (Ranchi City) Paras Rana told PTI that Bhagat's body was found hanging from a ceiling fan in a room at her residence.
The body has been sent to the Rajendra Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS) for post-mortem examination, he added.
"Prima facie, it appears that she died by suicide after going live on social media. The exact reason behind the incident is yet to be ascertained," another police officer said, adding that a detailed investigation had been initiated.
BJP demands Hemant Soren's resignation
The opposition BJP demanded the chief minister's resignation over the activist's death, while the JMM ally CPI(ML) Liberation sought a fair investigation.
Leader of the Opposition Babulal Marandi described Bhagat as a young tribal leader who fought for the rights of her community.
"She held Chief Minister Hemant Soren, the Pithoria police station in-charge, and Ajay Tirkey responsible for this," he said in a social media post.
He described it as "shameful and unfortunate" that a young woman who raised her voice for tribal rights was allegedly harassed to such an extent that she took her own life.
"Chief Minister Hemant Soren should immediately resign from his post," he added.
BJP state president Aditya Sahu alleged that Bhagat was deeply distressed by harassment by middlemen and associates of the chief minister, claiming this drove her to take the extreme step after going live on social media.
Sahu also questioned the police response, alleging that they had failed to intervene despite her statement during the Facebook Live session that she was going to die.
"If the police had acted immediately, perhaps her life would not have been lost," he said, demanding action against the police personnel concerned and those whose alleged statements had hurt the young leader.
Former chief minister Champai Soren described Bhagat's death as an irreparable loss to the tribal community.
Former chief minister Raghubar Das alleged that the state government was protecting land brokers.
The CPI(ML) Liberation, an ally of Soren's Jharkhand Mukti Morcha (JMM), expressed grief over Bhagat's death and demanded an impartial, high-level probe into the incident.
"The untimely demise of a tribal leader is heart-wrenching. The truth of the matter must surface, and the bereaved family should get justice," the party's state secretary, Manoj Bhakat, said.
He urged the state government to take the incident seriously and ensure an impartial investigation.

articles.text:
New Glenn's return to flight has slipped to January 2027, according to the internal memo, viewed by The Register, from Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, overshadowing the company's announcements of a new third stage and booster engine.

Blue Origin has been rebuilding after its New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in May, extensively damaging the launchpad.

A month later, the company's CEO, Dave Limp, said that Blue Origin "still plan[s] to fly again this year," which raised a few eyebrows in the space and rocket community. The detonation had pretty much destroyed the facility, and getting back into the launch business so quickly seemed optimistic.

That timetable has now slipped. In the memo, Limp praised the team's efforts but said: "We're proactively updating our anticipated launch date to January 2027."

A small slip given the damage, but one that leaves less breathing room before NASA's planned Artemis III demonstration mission, involving lunar technologies from Blue Origin and SpaceX, next year.

The delay emerged as the Bezos-backed company unveiled GS3, a third stage for New Glenn, designed for missions including direct injection into geostationary orbit and Earth-escape trajectories. The company said: "GS3 is already under contract for a cislunar mission with a government customer scheduled to launch in 2028."

Blue Origin says the stage is not required for its lunar lander architecture, although it could support sustained operations around the Moon.

The company also unveiled Northstar, a booster engine it says has half the parts and 30 percent less mass than its BE-4, while increasing thrust from 640,000 to 715,000 pounds-force.

The memo said the team had "found and fixed the issue that caused the anomaly," without elaborating. Limp said in August that the problem "originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines" and that existing engines would need retrofitting, but did not explain how the valve failed or what changes were required.

The memo added that the company would "continue sharing progress updates on Voyager ." ®

articles.title: India, EU conclude negotiations for association with Horizon Europe research programme
articles.text:
India, EU conclude negotiations for association with Horizon Europe research programme
India’s association with the EU’s €93.5-billion Horizon Europe programme will open up research funding and collaboration opportunities.
India and the European Union (EU) have concluded negotiations on New Delhi’s association with Horizon Europe, the EU’s €93.5-billion flagship research and innovation programme, ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s expected visit to Brussels for the conclusion of the India-EU trade deal.
The conclusion of the negotiations between the Indian side and the European Commission is an “important step” forward for EU-India relations, strengthening scientific cooperation, creating new opportunities in research, and deepening the bilateral strategic partnership, the Commission said on Friday.
This also clears the way for the signing of the association agreement, subject to the completion of the necessary procedures by both sides. Association is envisaged to begin in January 2027, the Commission said. India’s association will open up more opportunities for researchers, research organisations and businesses across Europe to collaborate with Indian partners and build scientific and technological links.
Also Read | Making the India-EU trade deal work for Tiruppur and Moradabad
Indian researchers to gain access to €93.5-billion EU research programme
Once the agreement is signed and the necessary procedures are completed by both sides, Indian researchers and organisations will be able to receive funding directly from Horizon Europe and lead collaborative projects under its Pillar II on “Global Challenges and European Industrial Competitiveness”. This is the largest part of the programme, which funds collaborative, multinational research and innovation projects tackling societal and technological issues such as health, digital, industry, space, climate, energy and bioeconomy.
Indian and European partners will be able to pool expertise, develop technologies and address shared challenges.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to travel to Brussels in mid-December for the formal signing of the India-EU free trade agreement, negotiations for which were concluded in January. The trade deal is expected to enter into force next year after it is ratified by the European Parliament.
Association with Horizon Europe is the closest form of cooperation offered by the EU to countries outside the grouping under the programme. This allows organisations in associated countries to participate on equal terms with EU counterparts in the areas of Horizon Europe covered by the agreement. In return, associated countries contribute financially to the programme.
“The agreement opens new opportunities for our businesses. Horizon Europe will help our researchers and innovators work together on what comes next. We want Europe and India to be partners in developing the technologies that will shape our future,” said Ekaterina Zaharieva, EU commissioner for startups, research and innovation.
India and the EU launched exploratory discussions on Horizon Europe in February, followed by formal negotiations in July. India-EU scientific cooperation builds on the Agreement for Scientific and Technological Cooperation, signed in 2001 and renewed until 2030.
Research and innovation are an integral part of the Joint India-EU Comprehensive Strategic Agenda to 2030, adopted at the India-EU Summit in January. The partnership has been strengthened through the bilateral Trade and Technology Council, which facilitates collaboration in key digital areas such as artificial intelligence, digital public infrastructure, semiconductors, high-performance computing, digital skills and sixth-generation wireless telecommunications.
India and the EU took a further step in collaboration on digital skills through the launch of the first-ever European Legal Gateway Office in India in February, aimed at facilitating safe and legal mobility to EU states in the ICT sector.
International cooperation is central to Horizon Europe, which runs from 2021 to 2027 and has a budget of €93.5 billion. A total of 23 non-EU countries are currently associated with Horizon Europe, including Canada, Egypt, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand, Norway, Switzerland, Ukraine and the UK. Negotiations for association have also been concluded with Australia.

DigiCert admits 16-month security lapse exposed customer information
articles.text:
DigiCert has admitted that a botched server migration left an internal system exposed to the internet for more than a year, allowing an unauthorized user to access customer data, including passports, driver's licenses, and other identity documents.

The certificate authority has begun notifying affected customers but has yet to disclose how many people had their information exposed.

In an email seen by The Register, DigiCert confirmed the compromised information included names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses. Some records may also have contained passports, driver's licenses, utility bills, or other identification documents.

"We are completing a review of identification documents to determine the specific individuals involved," DigiCert told those affected, adding that it would notify those people once the review was complete.

DigiCert's incident report traces the blunder back to February 2025, when an internal business system was moved from a VPN-protected network to a different availability zone. That change also opened the system up to the public internet, where it sat for more than 16 months without DigiCert realizing.

The archive used the same account management platform as DigiCert's customer-facing products, including a self-registration feature that was never supposed to be available on the internal system. This allowed outsiders to create accounts without multifactor authentication and, thanks to a separate permissions flaw, use them to browse archived customer records.

DigiCert found the unauthorized accounts on June 18, 2026, but initially dismissed them as harmless because they weren't assigned to an application. A security researcher raised the alarm about the account creation issue three days later, but it took until July 2 for DigiCert to shut it down.

Unfortunately, someone had already been poking around.

It wasn't until October 12 that DigiCert began investigating whether customer information had actually been accessed. On October 19, it confirmed that an unauthorized account had accessed a subset of archived records between June 27 and July 2.

DigiCert described the affected records as a "small proportion" of its archive but hasn't disclosed how many customers or individuals were caught up in the breach. The company did not respond to The Register’s questions at the time of publication.

DigiCert's postmortem makes for uncomfortable reading. The server move didn't get a proper security review, monitoring failed to pick up suspicious activity, and the access controls weren't much use against self-registered accounts. The company has since switched off self-registration, tightened network access, and added monitoring that might have come in handy a few months earlier.

Certificate authority operations, CertCentral, and DigiCert ONE were unaffected, the company said, adding that customer credentials and issued certificates remain secure. It also found no evidence that the unauthorized account had been used to issue, revoke, or validate certificates.

That’s good news for anyone worried about their certificates, but less so for those who handed DigiCert a copy of their passport. ®

Home Office cloud services contract may net AWS £1B
articles.text:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) looks set to win more than a billion pounds of UK taxpayers' money under a new Home Office contract for public cloud hosting.

A planning notice, published on October 30, covers the renewal of the department's public cloud services, to meet its current and future hosting needs. The estimated value is £881,621,007 ($1.18 billion), which passes £1 billion once VAT is included.

AWS won the existing contract with the Home Office in 2023 for about £450 million (c $603 million). The Register has asked the Home Office why the figure has risen so much, and will update this article if it responds.

Once awarded, the contract is expected to run from December 2027 to December 2029, with a possible extension to December 2031 (four years in total). A market engagement event for suppliers on the G-Cloud 15 Lot 1A procurement framework is scheduled for December 8, giving bidders the chance to pitch.

The Home Office would not say who else is being considered, saying it does not comment on ongoing procurement.

The notice lands as digital sovereignty becomes a bigger problem in the UK and across Europe, amid suspicion that US authorities have cut off access to American technology for political reasons. A survey found that about three-quarters of businesses in the UK, France, and Germany fear Washington could abruptly sever access to the US tech platforms they rely on.

Earlier this year, the Open Rights Group warned politicians that the UK is far too dependent on US technology companies to run critical operations.

Whitehall is mindful of its over-reliance on American hyperscalers. As The Register revealed in 2024, the Cabinet Office admitted - in an internal document seen by us - that the government’s negotiating power had been inhibited by vendor lock-in.

It said the "UK government’s current approach to cloud adoption and management across its departments faces several challenges" which combined result "in risk concentration and vendor lock-in that inhibit UK government’s negotiating power over the cloud vendors." It acknowledged "the existing dominance of AWS and Azure in the UK Government’s cloud services is set to continue."

A source at one supplier that works with the public sector said the UK administration was "failing to support UK [cloud] providers, it says they can’t meet scale and that is garbage." They claimed that in many cases the government people writing the tenders are advised by professional services companies to favor the hyperscalers. The professional services companies are then "rewarded" as migration or integration partners, our source claimed.

The UK government also pledged to steer more business to small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) in an action plan published last month. In August it added smaller, local suppliers to G-Cloud 15, though a place on the framework does not guarantee any business.

Pledges like this are nothing new, and they have largely come to nothing, as we reported in 2005, 2013, 2016, and 2018.

According to public sector intelligence platform BidSkim, AWS takes 75 percent of the government money on cloud contracts, worth about £1.22 billion ($1.6 billion). It estimates that Microsoft Azure has more contracts, but these are smaller and add up to £355 million ($475 million), while Google Cloud is on £47 million ($63 million) and Oracle Cloud $15 million ($20 million).

The Reg has asked AWS to comment. ®

articles.title: HT Exclusive: Contractors ignored workers’ warnings about weak structure, says FIR on Chawri Bazar collapse
articles.text:
HT Exclusive: Contractors ignored workers’ warnings about weak structure, says FIR on Chawri Bazar collapse
Construction worker Firoz alleged that the contractors insisted that the work continue, saying that making the changes would increase construction costs.
The contractors overseeing construction of the building that collapsed in Old Delhi’s Chawri Bazar on Thursday, killing at least two people, allegedly ignored warnings from workers about the poor quality of construction material and the structure’s inability to support another concrete slab, according to the first information report (FIR) registered in the incident.
In his statement to the police, complainant Firoz, a 37-year-old construction worker from Bihar who lives in Mandawali and survived the collapse, alleged that the contractors were repeatedly alerted about the structural concerns but insisted that the work continue, saying that making the changes would increase construction costs.
"We had informed the contractors that the lintel had not dried up and we cannot put another one.... to support the lintel, more cement and wood is required... but they asked us to continue saying that the cost would increase" Firoz said in the FIR read out to HT.
What the complainant alleged in the FIR
Deep Dive
The FIR names Tajuddin and Furkan as accused and invokes sections 105 (culpable homicidenot amounting to murder), 290, 125(a) (negligent act wirth respect to building)and 3(5) (common intention) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).
According to Firoz’s statement, he and other workers had been engaged by the contractors to carry out construction work on a plot measuring around 70 square yards. The building was being constructed in stages, and three concrete slabs (lanterns) had already been laid, he said.
Firoz, in the document said, that the workers were concerned about the quality of the construction and the amount of cement being used. He alleged that the existing slab was not sufficiently strong to bear the weight of another slab and that additional cement and construction material were required to provide adequate support.
However, instead of addressing their concerns, the contractors allegedly asked them to continue working.
The worker also told police that they had attempted to bring the matter to the owners’ attention. "However, they said that the contractors were handling the construction work so we should tell them" he said in the FIR adding that nobody paid heed to their warnings.
3 arrested in connection with building collapse
Around 9.30am on Thursday, Firoz and the other workers were carrying out construction work when the building suddenly collapsed, according to his statement.
The collapse trapped two of his fellow workers under the debris, while Firoz was at the rear portion of the building when the structure came crashing down. The incident left him among the survivors of the collapse.
In the early hours of Friday, Delhi Police arrested three contractors in connection with the Chawri Bazar building collapse case, officials aware of the matter said on Friday.
Police said the three men were arrested from Sirohi village in Faridabad’s Dauj tehsil.
Deputy commissioner of police (central) Rohit Rajbir Singh identified the accused as Siraj, Tajuddin and Furkan, all residents of the Ajmeri Gate area. Their full names were not immediately available.
Building collapsed in two stages
The arrests come amid questions over how construction continued at the site despite the building allegedly having no sanctioned plan and Delhi Police having alerted the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) about construction activity in the area nearly five months before the collapse.
The building, a ground-plus-three-floor structure in Gali Sitara near Chawri Bazar Metro station, collapsed in two stages around 9.30am on Thursday. The lintel of the third floor reportedly gave way while concrete work was underway, followed by the collapse of the remaining floors within 15 to 20 minutes. Two workers, Kishori, 40, and Sanjeet, 45, died, while two others sustained injuries.
MCD inaction flagged
The collapse also exposed serious enforcement lapses. In a letter dated June 15, the station house officer of Hauz Qazi police station had alerted the deputy commissioner of MCD’s City SP Zone about new residential construction spread over around 70 square yards at property number 4547-48 in Wali Sheesh Mahal, Ajmeri Gate, and sought action.
MCD acknowledged receiving the communication but said its subsequent inspection found the owner undertaking repair work that its maintenance department had advised in April. In its inquiry, the civic body alleged that the owner used the repair advisory as a cover to clandestinely undertake fresh construction on the second and third floors without the requisite permissions.
The MCD inquiry report also flagged the property's tax declarations, alleging that excess floor coverage had been declared with the mala fide intention of misleading the authorities and claiming protection under laws applicable to older structures.
The rescue operation on Thursday was hampered by the extremely narrow lanes of the walled city, which prevented heavy machinery from reaching the site. Fire personnel and other rescue teams had to rely largely on manual debris removal. Residents of neighbouring buildings were evacuated after police warned that one adjoining structure was in a precarious condition.
Chief minister Rekha Gupta ordered the immediate suspension of the junior engineer and assistant engineer concerned, a detailed inquiry and an FIR against the contractor. She also directed officials to ensure the best possible treatment for the injured and provide ex-gratia assistance to the victims' families.
Police are continuing their investigation into the construction activity and the circumstances leading to the collapse.
