“He is giving a version that he called them one by one, murdered them, and disposed of the bodies...we are verifying this...Six bodies have yet to be found as per the information provided by the accused,” Bengaluru police commissioner Seemanth Kumar Singh said.
Indushekar published Taana Varadari, a Kannada-English monthly tabloid, and ran a local YouTube news channel. The tabloid’s August 2026 edition identifies him as its editor and publisher.
“It is a very unfortunate incident...The investigation is on. The accused claims that he was humiliated by his wife’s side. It is definitely a twisted mind that has done the job. He has given the whereabouts of the bodies across the state,” Karnataka home minister Priyank Kharge told reporters.
Also Read | Bengaluru cab driver claims he killed wife, in-laws ‘over 15 to 20 days’: Police
Investigation is ongoing
Babasab Nemagoud, deputy commissioner of police (North), said a special team comprising three assistant commissioners of police had been formed. Around 50 personnel are involved in the investigation and the search for the bodies.
Police suspect Indushekar used a grinding stone to attack the victims and a car to move the bodies. Both have been seized.
A missing-person complaint filed on Thursday by Nalini’s mother alerted police, who zeroed in on Indushekar. The complaint was lodged at Srirampura police station.
According to preliminary accounts, after killing Sunitha, Indushekar allegedly wrapped her body in a cloth and took it to the Nandi Hills area. He is believed to have told neighbours she had gone on a trip with friends.
Later, he allegedly invited her brothers, Shivakumar and Shankar, to his house. Police suspect the two men were killed soon after they arrived. Indushekar allegedly killed the others after that.
Investigators are examining the sequence of events and how the bodies were moved to different locations. They also suspect chemicals were used to clean bloodstains inside the house.
The room where the killings allegedly took place sits above a row of shops. A narrow staircase leads up to it, and it has an iron-barred window.
Preliminary investigations suggest that frequent disagreements over Sunitha’s visits to her parental home, and her closeness to her mother and brothers, had strained the marriage.
“Relatives had attempted to reconcile the couple, but the disputes continued. Indushekar resented the involvement of his wife’s family in their marital disagreements,” an investigator, who did not want to be named, said.
Police are questioning the couple’s daughter. “We do not want to make any statements about her role in the case. She is currently being questioned. All I can say is that she is crucial to the case,” the investigator said.

SC seeks Kerala Congress response to contempt plea over objectionable post against CJI Kant
The Supreme Court sought responses from KPCC office bearers on a contempt plea over a deleted post calling for CJI Surya Kant’s resignation.
The Supreme Court on Friday sought responses from Kerala Pradesh Congress Committee (KPCC) office bearers on a petition seeking contempt of court action over an objectionable social media post against Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant, observing that the “independence of the judiciary” was not a matter of “political convenience”.
The bench of justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi said it would examine whether the deleted post, published by the party’s official X account, amounted to contempt of court and issued notice on the petition filed by advocate Vineet Jindal, who sought suo motu contempt action over the post published by INC Keralam on October 12.
The bench said, “Only the Constitution is supreme. No individual or political organisation stands above it,” as it emphasised that the authority of the court rests on the rule of law and does not require “political endorsement”. “Any attempt to undermine it needs to be dealt with an iron hand,” the court held.
The post addressed the CJI as “Dear Surya Kant” and called on him to resign, adding that the party would find a replacement who could handle law and order.
The post appeared against the backdrop of Opposition parties’ protest seeking the removal of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and their challenge to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR). The Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, had earlier sought a meeting with the CJI, which was declined.
The KPCC appeared through its lawyer and informed the bench that the post was published by a person in the media wing without the approval of KPCC president Sunny Joseph. The post was soon deleted, the person was removed, and an unconditional apology was issued by the committee.
The bench observed, “We have to examine whether it (apology) has come from the pen or the heart,” even as it exempted the KPCC office bearers from personal appearance on the next date of hearing.
Jindal said that the post was viewed by more than 10 million people, causing widespread damage to the reputation and authority of the judiciary. He pointed out that such a post by a political party could undermine public confidence in the institution.
The bench said, “Our judgments are always open to criticism, but freedom of expression cannot be a shield for intimidation or interference with the administration of justice.” The court said it would examine whether the material amounted to contempt of court and sought the assistance of Attorney General R Venkataramani. The court was also inclined to appoint an amicus curiae, while indicating the names of senior advocates Arvind Datar and Siddharth Agarwal.
Jindal wrote a letter to the CJI on October 13 seeking action against the KPCC post. His letter was converted into a writ petition.
Following the publication of the post, the two Supreme Court bar associations – the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) and the Supreme Court Advocates on Record Association (SCOARA) – condemned the demand for the CJI’s resignation.
The two associations issued resolutions stating that such a statement bordered on contempt as it undermined public confidence in the judiciary and amounted to interference in the administration of justice. Following this, SCBA joint secretary Meneesh Dubey issued a legal notice to KPCC president Sunny Joseph on October 16, seeking a response to the post.
Subsequently, on October 22, the KPCC president responded to the legal notice, stating that the post was published by Vijay Thottathil, a member of the KPCC Media Cell, “without the prior knowledge, approval or consultation of the KPCC leadership”.
Joseph said in his reply, “Neither I nor the leadership had authorised him to demand the resignation of the CJI or to suggest that the organisation would find a replacement.” Though the committee admitted that the party’s official account was used for such an “unauthorised communication”, it stated that this did not establish that its contents were approved by the leadership.
Thottathil has since been removed from his position and asked to issue a public apology for the publication. The response further said, “The KPCC disapproves of, expressly disagrees with and censures the language employed in the post. The demand for resignation and the suggestion of finding a replacement for the CJI were inappropriate and should not have appeared on an official party platform,” the response stated.
Jindal’s letter said, “The office of the Chief Justice of India is a constitutional judicial office and cannot be treated as one whose continuance is subject to the approval or displeasure of any political organisation.”
“Legitimate criticism must be distinguished from conduct that may undermine the authority of the court or interfere with the administration of justice. The distinction must be assessed in the light of the language used, its context, the circumstances of publication and its actual or reasonably apprehended effect,” he further said.
Meanwhile, the same bench that heard the matter on Friday is also examining a petition filed by the SCBA against Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut and journalist Nikhil Wagle over their derogatory posts against the CJI and the judiciary in relation to the October 12 events. The court directed Raut to appear in person, while Wagle was permitted to appear virtually.

articles.title: Are Pop-Ups here to stay in Bengaluru?
articles.text:
Are Pop-Ups here to stay in Bengaluru?
Bengaluru’s restaurant pop-ups increasingly celebrate regional cuisines, but chefs warn that too many fleeting events can dilute a restaurant’s identity.
Are pop-ups here to stay in Bengaluru? Until the early 2000s, the word “pop-up” was used mostly for retail shops. Google Trends reports that pop-up restaurants gained ground only around 2014. Today, restaurant pop-ups are common all over the world. In New Delhi, diners are willing to pay close to ₹1 lakh for the fleeting privilege of tasting a visiting Michelin-starred chefs foam and truffle dishes. In Mumbai, the figure is a bit lower for this particular social cachet but not by much.
Bangalore too has restaurant pop-ups; and yes, we too import celebrity chefs. But our heart lies elsewhere. More and more, Bangalore restaurants are championing the local over the global.
The Oberoi Bengaluru is an example. They focus on micro-cuisines and brands that fiercely protect their roots and cultural legacy. Over the last couple of years, they have brought down chefs such as Jigmet Mingur of Ladakh, the Singh sisters of Beluadeori; and restaurants such as Oota of Karnataka, Amar Khamar of Kolkata, and Rynsan of Shillong.
Round the corner, The Park Bangalore has featured cuisines from Nagaland, Ladakh (Chef Nilza Wangmo), Bastar in Chhattisgarh, Badaga food from the Nilgiris, Khasi food with Daki & Daphi and many more. “Every pop-up brings a fresh perspective through storytelling, celebrating the vibrant culture and diversity and transforming the act of eating into dining into an immersive experience that goes far beyond the palate,” says The Park’s general manager Kiron Kumar.
This does not mean that celebrity chefs don’t visit. All five-star hotels use celebrities as a way to increase footfalls into their restaurants. The Oberoi invited Michelin-starred Odette of Singapore, which chef Anirban said “was a vital masterclass for their staff.”
The Leela Palace Bengaluru specifically invites Michelin-starred restaurants such as Cenci from Japan, and Araya from Chile to take over Le Cirque, their fine-dining restaurant. In 2025, they had 3-Michelin-starred Italian chef Massimo Bottura visit and priced each dinner at over ₹50,000 per diner. The two dinners were sold out. “Restaurant pop-ups do two things for us,” said The Leela’s director of culinary, Bengaluru and South India, Simran Singh Thapar. “For the staff, it is a way to learn techniques and culinary protocols that they can carry forward. For example, how do visiting chefs think about ingredients, how do they plate dishes, how do they interact with diners and so on. For our patrons, it is a way to enjoy a world-class meal without the hassle of travelling to a foreign country, booking a table, waiting for it and so on. They can travel half an hour and enjoy a Michelin-starred meal that would not be accessible to them elsewhere.”
Some of my friends who paid ₹50,000 for the meal rationalized it as lower than the cost of an airline ticket to Italy.
That said, restaurant pop-ups raise many poignant questions. They are in a sense like Cinderella, arriving at the ball with great fanfare, and disappearing at the stroke of midnight. Pop-ups transform dining into a competitive sport, fuelled by quickly disappearing booking links, curated guest lists, and algorithmic FOMO. As chef Anirban of the Oberoi says, “A restaurant can easily slide into becoming just a temporary venue, rather than a living, breathing, and evolving dining destination that collaborates with brands. Over-indexing on pop-ups can quickly erode a restaurant’s core identity, culinary philosophy, and internal innovation.”
So what is the solution? Bangalore restaurant, Nila, may have an answer. Its chef-owner Rahul Sharma has taken an innovative approach to its menu. Rather than a single menu, it is intentionally rotational. So far, there have been three menus: inspired by Nagaland, Ladakh and Kerala. Next in line is the Sundarbans. “Every time we explore a region, we invite a chef from that part of the country to cook alongside us,” says Rahul. “It gives us an opportunity to bring the region’s ingredients, flavours, traditions and dishes to the table, interpreted through our own unique approach.”
To be fair, most stand-alone and long-standing restaurants in Bangalore at different price points like 13th Floor, Tandoor, 1947, Koshy’s or ITC’s Royal Afghan don’t do (and don’t need to do) pop-ups. People visit these restaurants for the predictable and comforting food. Some five-star hotels like the Taj West End rarely do pop-ups, preferring to have bar take-overs at its acclaimed restaurant Loya. My brother took my mother for her birthday meal to Loya and she thoroughly loved the food and cocktails.
Some hotels like JW Marriott Prestige Golfshire use pop-ups as a way to lure diners. A couple of years ago, I travelled two hours to have a pop-up dinner there by chef Gaggan Anand, whose Bangkok restaurant routinely tops “best of” lists. It was an exceptional memorable meal, well-worth braving the traffic. I still remember it.

articles.title: Fire breaks out at South Delhi Kia showroom; several injured
articles.text:
Fire breaks out at South Delhi Kia showroom; several injured
The fire has been brought under control, but a search operation is under way inside the showroom to check whether anyone is still trapped.
A fire broke out at a Kia car showroom in South Delhi's Saidulajab area on Friday afternoon, damaging several vehicles and leaving seven people injured. Around 12-15 people were also rescued from the building, an official said.
At least eight people, including two police personnel, were injured in the incident. Two people were admitted to a hospital with breathing issues, but were stable after receiving medical care. All eight injured have been discharged, officials said.
The fire has been brought under control, but a search operation is under way inside the showroom to check whether anyone is still trapped or has died in the incident, Deputy Magistrate Lakshya Singhal told PTI.
Also read | Fire breaks out at Gaffar Market in Delhi's Karol Bagh; 22 units deployed
"Around 3.45 pm, we received information that a Kia showroom opposite the metro station had caught fire. The fire department, police and other agencies were immediately mobilised. The SDM and the SHO also reached the spot," Singhal said.
Seven injured, several people rescued
Of the seven people injured in the fire, four were taken to MAX Hospital and three to Madan Mohan Malviya Hospital, Singhal said.
Also read | Over 150 locations across Delhi to get quicker fire response ahead of Diwali
Around 12-15 people were rescued from the building. Emergency teams placed ladders against neighbouring buildings to bring people down from the upper floors. Local residents also joined the rescue efforts, he added.
"As of now, there have been no casualties. The building is being searched to rule out any casualties," Singhal said.
Teams from the fire department, police, revenue department, Delhi Disaster Management Authority (DDMA), ambulance services and CATS were involved in the operation.
10 fire tenders rushed to spot
The Delhi Fire Services received a call about the blaze at around 3.47 pm and sent 10 fire tenders to the showroom initially. Firefighters and police personnel were deployed to bring the flames under control.
Thick black smoke could be seen rising from the showroom and spreading across the area. Several cars parked inside the building caught fire as the flames spread through the premises.
Traffic affected as crowds gather
The fire also drew a large crowd, with several passersby stopping to record videos on their mobile phones.
Traffic movement on the adjoining road was affected as onlookers gathered near the showroom. Police personnel intervened to clear the area and ensure that emergency vehicles could reach the spot.
The cause of the fire is yet to be determined.

articles.title: The fiery heat of the Deccan is all grit and no garden
articles.text:
The fiery heat of the Deccan is all grit and no garden
Today in India it has become fashionable to talk about gluten-free food as a way to overcome the diabetes that is rampant in our country.
One of the most interesting meals that I have had in Bangalore occurred about 20 years ago right after I first moved to the city in 2005. A friend and I visited Kamat Yatri Nivas, a lodging house with an in-house restaurant in the Majestic area. On the top floor we sat at a modest table and were served a Jolada Rotti Oota (lunch) with a choreographed sequence of dishes. What struck me about this meal was how healthy it was. We had a couple of kosambaris, which are essentially raw salads made with a combination of vegetables and pulses. The grated vegetables included radish, carrot, onion, cucumber, and chopped coriander, along with dals such as moong dal. Then there was the main part of the meal, which included Jolada Rotti made with jowar or sorghum flour. Incidentally, the way this word is said in Karnataka is different from the soft “roti” of North India. In South India, we hold the tongue firm for a much stronger “rotti”. Accompanying the jolada rotti was the badanekayi ennegayi, a spicy dish made with slit purple brinjals stuffed with a coconut-based gravy. There were a three powders or podis, including one made with shenga or peanuts. The sweets were not too sweet and included jaggery holige. Eating this meal made me realize that you could have a full lunch and not feel sleepy or tired, which is what usually happens to me after a rice-based South Indian feast.
Today in India it has become fashionable to talk about gluten-free food as a way to overcome the diabetes that is rampant in our country. The Uttara Karnataka meal that I had in Kamath Yatri Niwas was anchored by two millets: Jola and Sajji, or Jowar and Bajra (sorghum flour and pearl millet flour). To learn how the people of the Upper Deccan fashion these flours into flatbread, you only need to turn to YouTube, where there are a number of channels anchored by beautiful and simple women of North Karnataka with very specific recipes about how to cook the dishes. The one I like is simply called “Uttara Karnataka Recipes.”
The late great Suryanath Kamath, chief editor of the Karnataka State Gazetteer from 1981 to 1995, described the food habits of Uttara Karnataka in 1987 in simple yet detailed terms.
“The rural folk generally take three meals a day, the first meal at about eight O’clock in the morning before going to the fields consisting of jowar rotti. The second meal is taken in the afternoon mostly in the fields, also consisting of jowar rotti and a little rice occasionally, and the third meal of jowar rottis taken in the night at home.”
“Gruel (ambli) or nucchu made of jowar is also taken often for the morning meal or the second meal in the afternoon. Chatni, a paste consisting of chillies, salt and tamarind is invariably prepared. In summer more butter-milk is consumed and generally the consumption of milk is low in all the households. Groundnut oil is generally used for cooking. On special occasions and festivals sweets like holige, kadabu, payasa, shavige and huggi are prepared. Rice is occasionally eaten on festive days when they entertain guests. Most of the castes observe one day in a week as auspicious, by fasting on that day and non-vegetarians do not take the non-vegetarian food.”
“The daily food of the Brahmins, Lingayats and Jains include rice, jowar, pulse, curry, butter, curds, milk, etc. There is not much difference in food of the urban and rural households except that in the urban households a little more varieties of dishes are prepared and chapati instead of rotti, and also rice are consumed. The poor mostly consume maize which is relatively cheaper than jowar. Villagers use ama solada or vate kai in the place of tamarind in western taluks. Common side dishes prepared are amate (soup from pulses), palya or curry, usli of pulses, jhunaka, and chatni, both wet and dry (powder). In the urban areas, labourers go to hotels for the morning tiffin and generally take chapati or puri and bhaji. They carry with them the midday meal and eat at the working site.”
“The dishes of the Muslims do not differ much from the dishes of Hindus excepting the holiday dishes. The rich among Muslims take biryani mostly and the poor palav and pulses and mutton curry. Many rich families eat mutton daily. Except Boharas, Mehmans and members of four main divisions the Syeds, Shaiks, Mughuls and Pathans, almost all Muslims of Belgaum prefer mutton to beef and many local converts do not touch beef. An animal becomes lawful food for Muslims only if it is killed by cutting the throat and repeating the words ‘Bismillahi Allah o Akbar’ at that time. Fish and locusts may be taken without being killed in this manner.”
“The hotel preparations are idli, sambar, mirchi bhaji, chapati, puri, dosai, vade, srikhand, pedha, sira, etc. Belgaum is famous for kunda (a sweet prepared out of milk) and Gokak for sweet called kardantu. The people of the district prefer tea to coffee. It has almost become customary to drink tea in the morning before and after breakfast.”
So how is this region different? For one it is fiery, both in temperature and temperament. The standard cliche about people from North Karnataka is they are quick to anger. Their conversation is sharp and crackling, much like the land they inhabit. This is the sun-scorched open black-soiled plains of the Northern Deccan Plateau.
The landscape is unforgiving and the food reflects that grit. It is a cuisine of dry heat, wonderful textures, and a stubborn refusal – still – to hide behind the softening influence of coconut milk or cream, which is what is used in coastal areas. Today, even though creams and coconuts are available in abundance in Uttara Karnataka, the people here still prefer their age-old recipes, which to me is a blessing.

articles.title: Bank of England pours cold water on AI productivity boom
articles.text:
Despite the billions being thrown at artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered little in the way of productivity gains for UK businesses, according to the Bank of England.

In its latest Monetary Policy Report, the central bank found that AI has increased UK productivity by an estimated 0.5 percent over the past three years. That works out to just 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points of additional annual productivity growth since early 2024, hardly the economic revolution Silicon Valley has been promising.

"AI investment appears to be contributing somewhat to current demand strength, but so far there is only evidence of a modest AI-driven rise in UK productivity growth," the Bank said.

Even industries supposedly best placed to benefit from the technology have little to boast about. Productivity growth has improved in AI-heavy sectors such as information and communications, but has yet to exceed pre-pandemic averages.

That's not to say AI isn't doing anything for the British economy. The bank estimates that AI-related activity has accounted for just under a fifth of UK GDP growth since the beginning of 2026, though much of that appears to come from companies developing and deploying the technology rather than businesses becoming more productive by using it.

"The contribution to growth from AI to date appears to reflect activity in the upstream development and implementation of AI technologies rather than broader gains from their adoption elsewhere in the economy," the report said. In other words, selling AI is proving rather more lucrative than actually using it,

The bank also cautioned against giving AI too much credit for Britain's recent productivity improvements. Much of the increase appears to reflect businesses hiring fewer workers while output continues to grow, partly as companies unwind post-pandemic staffing decisions and respond to higher employment costs.

And despite predictions that AI will make vast swathes of the workforce redundant, firms responding to the Bank's Decision Maker Panel survey reported virtually no overall impact on employment so far. The technology is, however, making some employers less inclined to hire new staff or replace those who leave.

Other studies suggest businesses are still waiting for the payoff. A Gartner survey published last month found that while three-quarters of corporate board members expected AI to improve productivity and cut costs, just 3 percent of organizations had actually achieved their targets. Meanwhile, 38 percent were already over budget on AI spending, yet 85 percent planned to spend even more next year.

Another study involving nearly 6,000 executives, published in February, found that more than 80 percent of firms had seen no discernible impact from AI on either employment or productivity. Apparently, the answer to disappointing returns is to keep writing checks.

That growing disconnect between AI spending and actual returns has also caught the attention of financial watchdogs. The International Monetary Fund warned last month that the AI spending spree could come back to bite investors if the promised profits don't show up, potentially dragging the wider economy down with it.

The Bank for International Settlements sounded a similar alarm in June, comparing the current spending spree to the dotcom boom of the 1990s. Its concern is that tech giants are committing enormous sums to infrastructure on the assumption that AI will eventually deliver equally enormous returns, leaving them exposed if reality fails to cooperate.

However, AI is already making its presence felt in one area: prices. The Bank of England noted that surging demand for AI-related products, including memory chips, has pushed up export prices in China and other Asian economies, raising import costs for Britain.

So while businesses are still waiting for their AI-powered productivity windfall, the costs of the boom are already making their way through the economy.

The bank isn't writing off the technology just yet. Businesses surveyed expect AI to add around 0.9 percentage points to annual productivity growth over the next three years, with the gains split roughly equally between faster output growth and slower employment growth.

It seems the AI industry's most impressive productivity achievement is convincing businesses to keep opening their wallets. ®
articles.summary:
Despite the billions being thrown at artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered little in the way of productivity gains for UK businesses, according to the Bank of England.

articles.title: Police, mining authorities bound to register FIRs for theft of state-owned minerals, says NGT
articles.text:
Police, mining authorities bound to register FIRs for theft of state-owned minerals, says NGT
The NGT ruled that police and mining authorities must register FIRs for theft of state-owned minerals, saying payment of penalties does not bar criminal prosecution.
The National Green Tribunal (NGT) has ruled that local police and mining authorities are legally bound to register First Information Reports (FIRs) under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for theft of state-owned minerals, making it clear that payment of penalties for illegal mining does not exempt offenders from criminal prosecution.
Disposing of an application concerning illegal sand mining and storage in the Mahanadi riverbed at Chikhili village in Bargarh district, the NGT’s Eastern Zone Bench ordered the state government to initiate criminal proceedings against the alleged offender and recover environmental compensation for the ecological damage.
The NGT also directed the Bargarh Superintendent of Police and the Regional Officer of the Odisha State Pollution Control Board (OSPCB) to register separate FIRs against Prem Kishore Patel, who was allegedly carrying out illegal sand mining and large-scale storage in the Mahanadi riverbed at Chikhili under Ambabhona tehsil without a valid mining lease.
The bench, comprising judicial member Justice Arun Kumar Tyagi and expert members A Senthil Vel and Ishwar Singh, said that compounding of offences under Section 23A of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, or payment of administrative penalties does not preclude criminal proceedings for theft of minerals. Such criminal liability has to be dealt with independently.
Also Read: Reconsider plea for special bench on illegal mining cases, SC to Orissa HC
Relying on Supreme Court judgments in Lalita Kumari vs Government of Uttar Pradesh and State of NCT of Delhi vs Sanjay, the tribunal underscored the obligation of law enforcement agencies to register FIRs when information discloses a cognisable offence involving theft of state-owned minerals.
Shivaji Patel of Bargarh had filed an application before the NGT, alleging that Prem Kishore Patel had been carrying out illegal sand mining and large-scale storage in the Mahanadi riverbed at Chikhili under Ambabhona tehsil without a valid mining lease. He alleged that sand was extracted using suction pumps mounted on boats and supplied commercially to construction projects and brick manufacturing units in the region.
During a raid on June 22, 2024, enforcement officials had reportedly detected around 8,688 cubic metres of illegally stored sand. However, the applicant alleged that the authorities repeatedly compounded the violations by imposing minor penalties instead of initiating criminal prosecution or seizing the machinery used for illegal mining.
A joint fact-finding committee comprising the Bargarh Collector, a senior scientist from the OSPCB and the district Mining Officer found that Chikhili was not a notified sand source and that no mining permission had ever been granted there.
The tribunal observed that the administration’s claim of not finding active mining during monsoon inspections could not absolve it of responsibility for taking action against illegally extracted and stored sand and its continuing commercial trade.
Besides directing criminal action against the alleged offender, the NGT ordered the OSPCB to initiate proceedings for the assessment and recovery of environmental compensation.
The NGT also asked the director of Mines and Geology to ensure that all vehicles transporting minor minerals were fitted with operational GPS-based vehicle tracking systems and Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) tags. Vehicles without such tracking systems should not be allowed to operate for mineral transportation, while those found to be involved in illegal activities should be seized, it said.
The tribunal also directed the Odisha chief secretary to personally review compliance with mineral monitoring regulations at least once every quarter. Minutes of the review meetings and transparency reports must be uploaded on the state government’s official website.
It also said all illegally mined or stored river sand seized by enforcement agencies must be disposed of through public auction, with the proceeds deposited in an OSPCB fund earmarked exclusively for environmental restoration in the affected region..

articles.title: UK ministers seek powers to investigate when AI agents are let off the leash
articles.text:
The UK government is paving the way for rules requiring essential service operators and digital providers to guard against losing control of AI agents and report incidents when safeguards fail.

An amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which is passing through Parliament, would give ministers powers to regulate the deployment and reporting of agentic AI in certain organizations. The new clause was introduced during the bill's third reading in the House of Lords this week.

In an explanatory note, ministers outlined plans for safeguards, notification of affected organizations, preservation of evidence, and government-led incident reviews. The measures would require consultation and parliamentary approval through secondary legislation.

The move follows a series of incidents. Last month, OpenAI revealed that its agents repeatedly strayed beyond their intended scope, prompting the company to notify more than 100 organizations about the issues. That came after July's incident, in which an OpenAI agent accessed the internet and breached machine learning platform Hugging Face. The episode, and the potential for more damage from poorly designed AI agent deployments, have prompted MPs to question whether UK law can deal with such threats.

Speaking to The Register, Stuart Davey, a partner at law firm Pinsent Masons, described the clause as "quite novel." Rather than directly imposing new duties, it would allow ministers to introduce rules and investigatory powers covering regulated organizations. Davey said that could include powers "to look where there has been such an AI agentic compromise or issue, and do some things... appoint inspectors, enter and search premises, seize and retain documents." Under the proposals, the minister could confer certain powers on regulators, requiring action from targeted organizations.

Potentially affected organizations include gas and electricity suppliers, managed service providers, and cloud providers deploying AI agents for customers. Foundation model developers would not automatically fall within scope simply because they build the underlying technology.

"Where there's a security or operational compromise in relation to a relevant network or information system, that would seem to capture those managed service providers or cloud computing providers who are using AI, and there's that loss of control," said Davey. He advised cloud and managed service providers to track whether the proposed measures become law.

Evin McMullen, CEO and co-founder of AI identity and control infrastructure company AmanTrue, said the amendment recognizes loss of oversight or control as a security risk but does not itself impose new duties.

"The amendment allows future regulations to introduce investigatory and enforcement powers where an incident involves an AI agent, targeting organizations running essential digital services," he said.

"The deployer of an AI agent chooses its permissions, connects it to systems, and gives it access to data. When something goes wrong, the deployer is the party that will be expected to explain what happened.

"Accountability stays with the organization that put the agent into the system, and ultimately with executives and the board. Whether model builders are captured will depend on how the regulations are written and whether a builder sits in a regulated category or a regulated supply chain." ®

articles.title: Karnataka reports ethanol concentration in petrol up to 31.2%
articles.text:
Karnataka reports ethanol concentration in petrol up to 31.2%
The state government has asked the Union government to explain the ethanol concentrations found in the samples.
Petrol sold in seven Karnataka districts contained ethanol concentrations as high as 31.2%, with eleven of 14 samples exceeding the 20% blend specified under the E20 standard, according to the state government.
The government said the highest concentration was recorded in a sample collected from an Indian Oil Corporation Limited (IOCL) outlet, containing 31.2% ethanol. A sample of Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL)’s Power petrol had 30.5%, while another sample from the company recorded 27% and a BPCL Speed sample contained 26.5%, it added.
The samples were collected from fuel stations in Bengaluru, Kolar, Chikkaballapura, Bengaluru Rural, Ramanagara, Mangaluru and Tumakuru, covering IOCL, HPCL, BPCL, Nayara Energy, Shell and Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited, according to a state government statement. HT has reached out to the companies for a response and the story will be updated with their replies.
The statement said testing was conducted at the Shriram Research Institute in Bengaluru, measuring ethanol content using gas chromatography. It added that the results showed substantial differences not only between companies but also among samples from the same company.
Variations between samples
The statement said two IOCL samples recorded ethanol concentrations of 31.2% and 20.8%. It added that BPCL samples ranged from 19.9% to 26.5%, while Shell samples recorded 13.5% and 25.5%. The statement said that across all 14 samples, 11 exceeded 20%, the remaining three were below that level, including one at 19.9%.
The government said it first sent samples to the in-house laboratories of IOCL and BPCL. “The test reports issued by these laboratories did not disclose the ethanol content of the fuel, despite it being one of the prescribed testing parameters,” the statement said.
The state then commissioned independent testing at the Shriram Research Institute. The laboratory certificates attached to the statement record the ethanol concentrations in the samples, including 31.2% in an IOCL sample and 30.5% in an HPCL Power sample.
The government said the omission in the oil companies’ reports raised questions about transparency in fuel marketing. It added that the laboratory findings establish the ethanol content of the samples tested. They do not, by themselves, establish how widespread such concentrations are across the state’s fuel supply, the statement said.
Concerns over vehicle damage
The government raised concerns about the impact of higher ethanol blends on vehicles designed to operate with lower concentrations. It added that estimates suggest that 99% of India’s vehicles were not built to handle blends exceeding E20. The government said even vehicles sold after April 2023 are certified for ethanol blends of up to 20%.
The statement estimated that motorists lose ₹62,000 crore annually through lower fuel efficiency. That calculation assumes a 10% reduction in mileage, annual petrol consumption of 6,200 crore litres and a price of ₹100 a litre. It separately estimates annual repair costs for vehicle components at ₹39,000 crore. “With a conservative estimate, consumers are facing a hidden burden of nearly ₹1.01 lakh crore annually,” the statement said.
The government questioned whether fuel dispensing infrastructure was equipped to handle higher ethanol blends. It said most dispensing units at petrol stations were designed for fuel containing up to 15% ethanol and argued that the necessary upgrades might not have been made.
The state government has asked the Union government to explain the ethanol concentrations found in the samples. It sought clarification on the actual blend being supplied to consumers and sought action against oil marketing companies found selling petrol containing over 20% ethanol.
The state government demanded that petrol stations across the country display the ethanol content of the fuel they sell and allow consumers to choose between available blends.
It added that it would continue testing fuel samples and publish the results. It cited the Motor Spirit and High Speed Diesel (Regulation of Supply and Distribution and Prevention of Malpractices) Order, 2005, which provides for action against malpractices in fuel supply and distribution.

Speaking to reporters after the meeting, which was also attended by Omar Abdullah, Farooq said the party remained united, termed reports suggesting a split within the National Conference baseless and assured that the concerns raised by party legislators would be addressed.

articles.title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
articles.text:
I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.

I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.

Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself. 

But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.

With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.

The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.

When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said.

Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.)

You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger.

In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle.

The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.

Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI. 

But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she said when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care.

Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.

articles.title: Britain's tech ambitions depend on minerals made in China, MPs warn
articles.text:
Britain's ambitions for AI, advanced chips, and clean energy rest on mineral supply chains dominated by China, and MPs say they cannot establish whether ministers have a credible plan to reduce that dependence.

The House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee has set ministers ten tests for securing critical minerals. Its verdict is hardly glowing – it cannot be confident the government passes any of them.

The tests cover whether ministers know which industries and technologies need protecting, what minerals they require, where supplies could be disrupted, and how domestic production, overseas partnerships, skills, and financing will close the gaps.

In a report published today, the committee warns that diversifying supplies will take ten to 15 years, and will require sustained investment and cooperation with allies. Completely cutting China out is neither realistic nor desirable, it says. Leaving Beijing with so much leverage is another matter.

Critical minerals underpin everything from batteries and semiconductors to datacenters and military equipment. The designation reflects their economic or security importance and vulnerability to supply disruption, rather than membership of an especially exclusive geological club.

The UK – like pretty much all major industrialized economies including the US, the EU, Japan, and India – is almost entirely dependent on imports of these materials and mineral products. But digging up more ore outside China would solve only part of the problem. The bigger bottleneck is processing.

Citing International Energy Agency figures, the committee says China is the leading refiner for 19 of 20 strategic minerals, with an average market share of 70 percent. A different flag over the mine does not necessarily mean a different route through the refinery.

The exposure extends beyond chips and batteries. As The Register reported in August, erbium is used to amplify signals in fiber-optic links, while yttrium goes into components including ceramic capacitors. IEEE Spectrum warned that China effectively monopolized the processing of both into the industrially usable materials manufacturers need.

That concentration has already caused disruption. China's rare earth export controls in April 2025, introduced following US tariffs, rippled through manufacturing supply chains and forced temporary automotive plant closures. British manufacturers can suffer even when Britain isn't the intended target.

The committee also highlights gallium and germanium, used in advanced semiconductors for radar, communications, and electronic warfare. China accounts for 95 percent and 93 percent of their global production respectively, according to the report [PDF].

Beijing flexing its leverage over chip materials is not new. China announced export licensing requirements for gallium and germanium in July 2023 amid tightening Western restrictions on semiconductor technology.

Yet MPs say the government has not clearly identified which domestic industrial and technological capabilities it wants to protect, making it difficult to determine which supply chains deserve priority.

Nor do import statistics reveal the whole exposure. Minerals can arrive inside batteries, magnets, and other manufactured components, disappearing from view as individual materials. Businesses themselves may not know precisely what lies several layers down their supply chains.

The committee wants confidential mapping and stress-testing with firms in critical sectors, followed by joint purchasing arrangements with allies to give new mining and refining projects dependable customers.

Committee chair Liam Byrne said: "Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy. We cannot re-arm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.

"Yet sixteen years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed. We don't know enough about what minerals we need or where to find them. Our energy costs make processing uneconomic, we're exporting valuable metal waste, and our public finance institutions are shackled by outdated rules."

More than a shopping list

The committee's five-part prescription is to identify the capabilities Britain must protect, map their mineral needs, expand domestic mining, processing, and recycling, pool purchasing power with allies, and establish a dedicated financing facility.

The proposed facility would bring together public funding bodies to back projects through grants, equity, loans, guarantees, and long-term purchase agreements.

"We're never going to eliminate Chinese minerals from our supply chains. But it's foolish to leave Britain exposed to economic coercion when we could be building alternative supplies," Byrne said.

"That's why we need a new Critical Minerals Finance Facility with the financial firepower to invest in new mines, processing plants and recycling, working with our allies to share the costs."

The report argues that existing institutions leave gaps, particularly for early-stage projects. It recommends expanding UK Export Finance's remit and allowing British International Investment to take equity stakes in overseas mineral projects.

Long-term purchasing commitments and price guarantees could help keep strategically important projects commercially viable despite volatile mineral prices.

There is also material closer to home. The report says 80 percent of UK metal products classified as waste are exported. MPs want better sorting and separation infrastructure, alongside more detailed trade data to establish exactly what valuable scrap is leaving the country.

For domestic projects, they recommend designated critical mineral clusters with permitting deadlines, help navigating approvals, energy support, and priority grid access.

Stockpiles could provide a short-term buffer too. The committee calls for an initial reserve covering approximately 60 days of minerals needed for defense capabilities, while stressing that warehouses are no substitute for diversified supply.

None of this offers a quick escape from dependence on China. The committee's argument is that Britain needs to decide what it must protect, work out what those industries actually consume, and help finance alternatives before the next disruption.

"De-risking even a prudent proportion of our supplies will take over a decade. Britain cannot afford to drift," Byrne said. "We must act now before dangerous dependencies become strategic liabilities." ®

articles.title: NHS wants a second opinion on Palantir's glowing self-assessments
articles.text:
NHS England CEO Sir Jim Mackey plans to tell Palantir to clear future claims about its Federated Data Platform's benefits with his team – although he admits that could be difficult to enforce.

Speaking to the Health and Social Care Committee this week, Labour MP Ben Coleman noted that NHS England had cautioned against attributing improvements directly to the platform, but said newly appointed Palantir UK senior vice president Tom Watson "is making claims that [Palantir] is making a difference, and that it's due to Palantir that changes are taking place."

Responding, Mackey said he would write to Palantir and "tell them that they have to share with us and clear with us any benefits claimed in the future."

But getting Palantir to comply could be another matter. "They should share them with us, but contractually, it looks hard to enforce," Mackey said.

The planned letter follows repeated questions about the evidence NHS England and Palantir have used to promote the Federated Data Platform (FDP). NHS England awarded the £330 million contract to a Palantir-led consortium in November 2023 to help improve planning and efficiency.

In July, campaign group Foxglove wrote to the UK health minister questioning figures used in Parliament to justify the contract. The Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) also began examining the evidence.

NHS England had said that as of June, 139 trusts used the platform, with 137 reporting benefits. It said an Inpatient Care Coordination Solution tool based on the FDP had helped hospitals perform procedures on an additional 111,589 patients. However, a Freedom of Information request later found that nearly a third of NHS trusts using Palantir's health data platform were performing fewer patient procedures than before it went live.

Later that month, the OSR said NHS England had accepted that it needed to communicate its claims about FDP performance more clearly.

The regulator noted that NHS England had published on its website a caveat saying that it could not "draw conclusions about cause and effect as other variables have not been controlled for."

Last month, Watson, the former deputy leader of the Labour Party, sought to rebut what he described as misinformation about the FDP, repeating the statement that 137 trusts were already reporting benefits without mentioning the caveats.

In a statement on X, Watson said the OSR had pointed out that there had not yet been a study on the FDP that controls for other factors like staffing level changes or industrial action. "That's a fair note of caution."

In a prepared video, he said Northampton General Hospital, University Hospitals of Derby and Burton, and Chelsea and Westminster Hospital had all produced figures showing they are benefiting from using the platform.

"Can we prove that every one of those procedures happened because of our software? No. But does that mean we should ignore what the hospitals are telling us? Of course not," he said.

In February 2026, NHS England awarded a contract to Imperial College Projects to independently evaluate the FDP. The findings are not expected until after ministers decide whether to extend the contract, which currently ends in March 2027. ®

NHS England CEO Sir Jim Mackey plans to tell Palantir to clear future claims about its Federated Data Platform's benefits with his team – although he admits that could be difficult to enforce.

articles.title: Safari's Autofill feature may be distorting time
articles.text:
The autofill feature of Apple's Safari browser appears to be suffering from a date handling error that occasionally leads it to supply an incorrect credit card expiration date when filling out forms.

The supposed issue has been a sore spot for Apple customers dating back at least to 2017, when the author of an Apple Community forum post complained about changes to the month field in the Autofill credit card expiration date when moving between time zones.

"I've noticed for the last year or so, whenever I travel from Eastern time zone (my home) to Central time zone or even Pacific time zone that my credit card expiration date month changes in Safari Autofill," the Safari user wrote.

Another post in 2021 raised similar concerns.

"I don't know how to reproduce this," the author wrote. "Every few months Safari on any of my devices changes the expiration month of all of my stored credit cards by decreasing the month by 1, for example instead of 10/2029 it changes it to 09/2029."

Three years later, another person posting to Apple's Community forum reported the same issue.

"For a few years now every time I use Autofill on my computer my credit cards (ALL of them) always have their expiration dates change one month earlier," the 2024 post says. "I thought it was just a glitch on my computer but I bought a new computer and didn't transfer anything from my old one and it is still doing it."

An unrelated Autofill bug report from 2024 suggests that if there is an issue, it resides in Apple-owned Safari code rather than Safari's open source WebKit engine.

Wherever the bug may reside, Safari's unreliable handling of credit card dates has kept a complaint-filled Reddit thread going for four years. And the reported month-shifting has been noted in other threads, too.

The Register was unable to reproduce the described behavior, but a reader insists it's still a problem.

"The Safari AutoFill feature sometimes fills in the credit card expiration date wrong," the reader explained. "My credit card expires in December, but sometimes Apple helpfully enters November."

"To be clear, the card is stored correctly when inspected in Settings," our tipster added. "The off-by-one error only happens when filling out a form in Safari, and not consistently."

One possible way this might happen is if the Safari Autofill code implemented the expiration date using Swift's DateComponent type and stored it as a Calendar object with UTC as the TimeZone identifier. Doing so would anchor the date to a specific time. If the date components were extracted in Pacific Time, the value would be represented as eight hours ahead (PST). So 9/1/2027 at 00:00 would appear as 8/31/2027 at 16:00.

Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but we're told Apple's Help Desk – or "Helpless Desk" as our source put it – advised clearing the browser cache and re-entering details of the affected credit card.

If that works, it suggests Safari's handling of cached data in the context of Autofill dates may need to be revisited.

Apple does not maintain a public bug database and the community-maintained OpenRadar sheds no light on these reports. ®

articles.title: How Far Can a Trainable Frequency Move? Resolution, Grids and Coupling in Trainable-FrequencyQuantum Models
articles.text:
arXiv:2602.23409v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Trainable-frequency quantum models train the prefactors of their encoding gates so that the circuit's frequencies can move onto the target's. From the unit start of prior work, training rarely reaches a target more than one resolution step away. We show that the target-driven part of the prefactor gradient is a weighted sum of slopes of the overlap $\sin u/u$, where $u$ is the model-target frequency distance scaled by the window half-width. This gives each frequency a reach: under gradient flow, an isolated real frequency whose coefficient adapts optimally reaches its target from within half a step, for every target at least one step from zero frequency; with a fixed coefficient, a phase-dependent barrier can stop it. A ternary prefactor grid places a model frequency within half a step of every band frequency, with logarithmically many encoding gates. Single-frequency circuits trained with Adam and jointly trained amplitudes behave as predicted: inside the first side lobe, a frequency starts toward its target exactly when in phase with it in 98% of runs, and only 11 of 768 frequencies starting beyond the lobe reached their target. With several frequencies, the grid start raised successful fits on synthetic targets from 69% to 84% against the best random start. With many target frequencies, least squares on the fixed grid fits near-perfectly, but the circuit does not reach the coefficients; training the prefactors narrows this shortfall, but with 8 and 24 target frequencies, training the fixed grid ten times longer fitted better. On real series, training the frequencies improved held-out $R^2$ at equal budget by 0.010--0.045 on four of seven series, but a classical screen did not separate these from the others. A classical model with independently trainable frequencies shows the same dependence on the start; our results describe how to train such models, not an advantage of the circuit.

articles.title: Alignment Collapse Under KV Cache Quantization: Diagnosis and Mitigation
articles.text:
arXiv:2606.09864v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Key-value (KV) cache quantization is widely used to reduce LLM inference memory, yet existing evaluations focus only on perplexity and accuracy without assessing the safety impact. In this study, we explore alignment preservation under KV cache quantization. Across eleven instruction-tuned models (3.8B-72B) and five benchmarks (1,894 prompts), we find that low-bit quantization can silently destroy safety alignment: Mistral-7B loses 15.2% of its refusals at only 1.03x perplexity, and no universal safe bit-width exists, with sharp model-specific phase transitions invisible to standard metrics. We identify that the root cause is geometric: safety features occupy a low-dimensional activation subspace $10^2$-$10^3\times$ more vulnerable to quantization noise than the full representation space perplexity averages over. We propose Per-Channel Reduction (PCR), a diagnostic that classifies each model into one of three mechanistic failure modes: outlier-crushes-safety, where safety lives in non-outlier channels collaterally damaged by outlier-driven scale factors; outlier-as-safety, where safety overlaps outlier channels and finer granularity cannot rescue it; and multi-layer dilution, where safety is distributed across many layers and per-layer fixes fail. PCR predicts the correct mitigation direction on all nine primary models and one held-out model from an independent family using 20 calibration prompts. PCR generalizes across unseen prompts, models, and quantizer families, including production quantizers (KIVI: up to 97.2% recovery) and rotation-based quantization (QuaRot-style Hadamard), succeeding where attention-based allocation methods fail. The resulting training-free protocol, requiring ~35 GPU-minutes, recovers up to 97% of lost alignment at under 1% latency and minimal memory overhead, addressing vulnerabilities confirmed in production vLLM serving with FP8 KV cache on NVIDIA GPUs.

articles.title: Value Over Language Model: Detecting Original Contribution in Writing
articles.text:
arXiv:2609.00700v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLMs have been rapidly adopted across writing tasks, prompting the development of tools for detecting LLM-generated text. Yet, these tools largely measure how much of a document's surface text was written by an LLM and aren't fundamentally designed to measure how much of the information content or ideas originated from the LLM itself rather than being supplied by the user in the prompt. In this work, we design a framework that measures how much value a person adds on top of what a language model could have easily produced by itself. The method requires no training or labeled data and never scores the document's surface text, insulating it from stylistic confounders. Instead, it extracts the document's content at increasing levels of granularity, uses an LLM to reconstruct the document from each partial representation, and compares these reconstructions with those produced from the task description alone. We call this framework Value Over Language Model (VOLM), which measures a document's contribution relative to a replacement-level document that an LLM could produce from the task description alone. We evaluate VOLM with a specific instantiation of this framework across three domains: news articles, ICLR peer reviews, and argumentative essays. VOLM separates human-authored documents from matched LLM-generated documents produced from generic task descriptions, while remaining substantially invariant to content-preserving transformations, including LLM-based reconstruction and round-trip translation. We further find that increasingly constrained content extractors reduce residual differences between LLM-generated and humanized text, demonstrating the importance of disentangling informational content from stylistic variation. We hope these results encourage further work on specialized instantiations of the framework and on assessing human contributions in LLM-assisted writing more generally.

articles.title: Agentic Abstention: Do Agents Know When to Stop Instead of Act?
articles.text:
arXiv:2606.28733v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM agents are expected to act over multiple turns, using search, browsing interfaces, and tools to complete user goals. Yet not every goal is well specified or achievable in an available environment. In such cases, a reliable agent should recognize that further interaction is unlikely to help and abstain from additional tool calls. We define Agentic Abstention, the problem of deciding when an agent should stop acting under uncertainty. Unlike standard LLM abstention, which is usually evaluated as a single-turn answer-or-abstain decision, agentic abstention is a sequential decision problem: an agent can answer, abstain, or gather more information at each turn, and the need to abstain may only become clear after interacting with the environment. We study this problem across web shopping, terminal environments, and question answering, evaluating 13 LLM-as-agent systems and 2 agent scaffolds on more than 28,000 task instructions. Our results show that the main challenge is not only whether agents can abstain, but also when they abstain. Some agents never abstain when they should, while others do so only after many unnecessary interactions. This gap is especially large on tasks where the instruction appears feasible until the environment reveals otherwise (e.g., no valid result matches the instruction). We further find that model scale, reasoning, and agent scaffolding affect abstention in different ways, where larger or more capable models sometimes perform worse at timely abstention. Finally, we introduce CONVOLVE, a context engineering method for improving agentic abstention that distills interaction trajectories into reusable stopping rules. On held-out WebShop tasks, CONVOLVE substantially improves timely abstention without updating model parameters, raising Llama-3.3-70B's timely recall rate from 26.7 to 57.4. Our dataset and code are available at https://agentic-abstention.github.io.
